The short gastric veins (vasa brevia) drain the fundus of the stomach into the splenic vein, which then joins the superior mesenteric vein to form the portal vein. In portal hypertension, these short gastric veins become dilated and hypertensive, contributing to gastric varices that can rupture and cause life-threatening upper GI hemorrhage. The other options: hepatic vein hypertension occurs in Budd-Chiari syndrome/right heart failure; inferior phrenic, renal, and suprarenal veins drain into the inferior vena cava (systemic circulation) and are not part of the portal system affected by cirrhosis.
subject: GI

text: An 18-year-old man is brought to the emergency department 30 minutes after a motorcycle collision. He has lost a significant amount of blood. His pulse is 120/min, and blood pressure is 90/70 mm Hg. Physical examination shows a severe laceration of the left calf. Rapid infusion of 0.9% saline is started to restore his vascular volume deficit. The solid curves in the graph show the relationship between right atrial pressure and cardiac output (cardiac function curve). The dashed lines show the relationship between cardiac output and right atrial pressure (vascular function curve). Point X is the preinfusion equilibrium point. Which of the following is the most likely new cardiac and vascular equilibrium point following the infusion?
explanation:
This patient has hemorrhagic shock from a motorcycle accident. The rapid infusion of 0.9% saline increases intravascular volume (preload), which increases right atrial pressure (RAP). According to the Frank-Starling mechanism, increased RAP increases ventricular end-diastolic volume, increasing stroke volume and cardiac output. On a cardiac function curve (cardiac output vs. RAP), volume expansion shifts to a point with higher RAP and higher CO. Simultaneously, the vascular function curve (which represents venous return as a function of RAP) shifts rightward because the mean circulatory filling pressure increases with volume expansion. The new equilibrium point (intersection of the two curves) would be at a higher RAP and higher CO compared to point X (the preinfusion equilibrium).

**Distractors:** Options showing lower right atrial pressure are incorrect because saline infusion expands intravascular volume and increases preload, thereby raising RAP. Options showing lower cardiac output are incorrect because increased preload increases ventricular end-diastolic volume and stroke volume via the Frank-Starling mechanism. An option showing higher RAP with lower CO would imply cardiac pump failure rather than successful volume resuscitation. An option showing unchanged RAP with higher CO would suggest increased contractility without volume loading, which is not the primary effect of saline infusion.
subject: Cardiovascular

text: A 28-year-old man comes to the physician because of a 2-day history of an abscess at the site of a splinter on his right index finger. The leukocytes in this abscess initially localized to the site of inflammation because of an endothelial adhesion molecule that binds ligands on the surface of the leukocyte. Which of the following molecules is the most likely cause of the adhesion to the endothelial surface at the site of inflammation?
explanation: Leukocyte recruitment to sites of inflammation is a multi-step cascade: rolling → activation → firm adhesion → transmigration. The initial step — leukocyte rolling along the endothelium — is mediated by selectins. P-selectin (stored in Weibel-Palade bodies of endothelial cells) and E-selectin (induced by cytokines like TNF and IL-1) are expressed on endothelial cells and bind to sialyl-Lewis X and other carbohydrate ligands on leukocytes. This loose tethering slows leukocytes down (rolling), allowing them to be activated by chemokines presented on the endothelial surface, leading to integrin activation and firm adhesion (mediated by ICAM-1 on endothelium binding to LFA-1/Mac-1 integrins on leukocytes). Cadherins mediate cell-cell junctions (not inflammation). Extracellular matrix proteins and proteoglycans are structural components. G proteins are intracellular signaling molecules.
subject: General Principles

text: A 25-year-old man is lost in the desert for 1 week with an ample supply of water but no food. Which of the following changes in enzyme activities and regulatory molecule concentrations in liver is most likely in this patient? Fructose Glucose Phosphoeno/pyruvate Pyruvate 2, 6-bisphosphate 6-phosphatase Carboxykinase Kinase ○A) ↑ ↑ ↑ ↓ ○B) ↑ ↑ ↓ ↓ ○C) ↑ ↓ ↓ ↑ ○D) ↓ ↑ ↑ ↓ ○E) ↓ ↑ ↓ ↓ ○F) ↓ ↓ ↑ ↑ ○G) ↓ ↓ ↓ ↑ ○H) ↓ ↓ ↓ ↓
explanation:
In the fasting/starvation state (1 week without food), the liver shifts from glycolysis to gluconeogenesis to maintain blood glucose. Fructose-2,6-bisphosphate (F-2,6-BP) is a potent allosteric activator of phosphofructokinase-1 (PFK-1, glycolysis) and inhibitor of fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase (gluconeogenesis). In starvation, glucagon ↑ and insulin ↓ lead to decreased F-2,6-BP levels, which reduces glycolysis and promotes gluconeogenesis. Glucose-6-phosphatase and PEP carboxykinase (PEPCK) are key gluconeogenic enzymes whose expression and activity increase. Pyruvate kinase (a glycolytic enzyme) is inhibited by glucagon via phosphorylation and decreased gene expression. Thus: F-2,6-BP ↓, G-6-Pase ↑, PEPCK ↑, Pyruvate kinase ↓ — which corresponds to option D.

Distractors: Options A–C incorrectly show increased fructose-2,6-bisphosphate, which is characteristic of the fed/insulin-dominant state, not starvation. Options C, F, G, and H incorrectly show decreased glucose-6-phosphatase or PEPCK, failing to recognize that gluconeogenic enzymes are upregulated during fasting. Options C, F, and G incorrectly show increased pyruvate kinase, which is inhibited during starvation to prevent glycolytic flux. Option H (all decreased) is incorrect because gluconeogenesis must remain active to maintain euglycemia.
subject: General Principles

text: A 28-year-old African American man comes to the physician because of a 3-month history of mild fatigue and weakness; he has had a 4.5-kg (10-lb) weight loss during this period. He also has a 6-month history of dry cough associated with chest pain and shortness of breath. The patient is married with two children, ages 2 and 3 years. He says that no one else at home has similar symptoms. He is a carpenter. He has several pets, including a dog, two cats, and a bird. He spent a week in Mexico approximately 1 year ago. He has smoked one-half pack of cigarettes daily for 10 years. He is 178 cm (5 ft 10 in) tall and weighs 70 kg (154 lb); BMI is 22 kg/m². Mild wheezes are heard. Physical examination shows no other abnormalities. A chest x-ray shows bilateral hilar adenopathy and right paratracheal node enlargement. Biopsy specimens obtained via fiberoptic bronchoscopy show noncaseating granulomas. Test results of the biopsy specimen for acid-fast bacilli and fungi are negative. Which of the following is the strongest predisposing risk factor for this patient's condition?
explanation:
This patient has sarcoidosis, a multisystem granulomatous disorder of unknown etiology characterized by noncaseating granulomas. The presentation (bilateral hilar adenopathy, right paratracheal lymphadenopathy, cough, chest pain, dyspnea, noncaseating granulomas, negative AFB and fungal stains) is classic. In the United States, African American ethnicity is the strongest known risk factor for sarcoidosis, with a 3-4 times higher incidence and more severe disease compared to Caucasians.

**Distractors:**
- **A) Employment:** Carpentry may involve inhalational exposures, but occupational risk is not as strongly established as ethnicity.
- **C) Gender:** Sarcoidosis is slightly more common in women, but gender is a weaker predisposing factor than African American ethnicity.
- **D) Living with pets:** No established association exists between pet ownership and sarcoidosis risk.
- **E) Recent travel to Mexico:** Endemic-region travel raises concern for fungal infections (e.g., coccidioidomycosis, histoplasmosis), which typically produce caseating granulomas rather than the noncaseating granulomas seen here.
- **F) Smoking history:** Smoking is not a major risk factor for sarcoidosis.
subject: Multisystem

text: A 10-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department 30 minutes after sustaining injuries in a skateboard accident. His vital signs are within normal limits. Physical examination shows tenderness to palpation over the right wrist. An x-ray shows a fracture of the right radius and ulna. He is treated with cast immobilization extending over the right elbow. He is no longer able to move his forearm muscles. Which of the following is most likely to occur in the immobilized muscles after 3 weeks in the cast?

options.text: Increased production of vascular endothelial growth factor

explanation: After 3 weeks of cast immobilization and muscle disuse, skeletal muscle undergoes profound atrophy. The decreased metabolic demand from inactivity leads to reduced capillary density (decreased capillarity) through capillary regression — a process called "capillary rarefaction." This occurs because existing capillaries are pruned back when the shear stress and metabolic signals that normally maintain them are absent. VEGF production decreases (not increases), and total blood flow decreases (not increases). Intracellular PO₂ and myoglobin oxygen saturation are more reflective of acute exercise or ischemia rather than chronic disuse. The metabolic rate of muscle decreases with disuse. Adenosine concentration would not chronically increase in immobilized muscle. The net effect is a match between reduced metabolic demand and reduced vascular supply.
subject: MSK/Skin

text: A previously healthy 12-year-old girl is brought to the physician because of a 1-week history of brief generalized tonic-clonic seizures. Her family recently emigrated from Mexico. Physical examination shows no abnormalities. A CT scan of the head shows multiple calcified nodules and some cysts. The most likely cause of her seizures is infection with which of the following causal organisms?
explanation: This patient has neurocysticercosis, the most common parasitic infection of the CNS worldwide, caused by the larval stage of Taenia solium (pork tapeworm). Recent emigration from Mexico (an endemic area), presentation with new-onset seizures, and CT showing multiple calcified nodules and cysts are highly characteristic. The cysts contain the scolex of the larva (Cysticercus cellulosae) and eventually calcify over years, leaving characteristic "punched-out" calcifications on imaging. The diagnosis is confirmed by serology and characteristic imaging findings. Toxoplasma gondii causes ring-enhancing lesions on CT, typically in immunocompromised patients, and lesions do not calcify in the same pattern. Tuberculosis and cryptococcosis would present with meningitis rather than multiple parenchymal calcified cysts. Herpes simplex encephalitis causes temporal lobe involvement. Bacterial causes of meningitis (Listeria, S. pneumoniae) present acutely with meningeal signs.
subject: Behavioral/Nervous & Special Senses
concept_fingerprint: neurocysticercosis Taenia solium seizures calcifications endemic

text: A 24-year-old man comes to the physician because of nasal congestion, a watery nasal discharge, and sneezing. He says that these symptoms happen each spring, when grass and tree pollens are abundant. Which of the following types of drugs is most likely to be effective in relieving these symptoms in the short term?
explanation:
This patient has seasonal allergic rhinitis (hay fever) triggered by grass and tree pollens. The primary symptoms (nasal congestion, watery rhinorrhea, sneezing) are mediated by histamine released from mast cells and by increased parasympathetic activity. For short-term relief of nasal congestion, α1-adrenergic agonists (e.g., oxymetazoline, phenylephrine, pseudoephedrine) are the most effective drug class. They cause vasoconstriction of the nasal vasculature by stimulating α1-adrenergic receptors on vascular smooth muscle, reducing mucosal edema and secretions. Antihistamines (H1 blockers) also help but are more effective for sneezing and itching than congestion. β-adrenergic agonists target bronchial smooth muscle (asthma/COPD) and would not relieve nasal congestion. β-blockers could worsen symptoms. Nicotinic agents have no role in allergic rhinitis.

**Distractors:** α-Adrenergic antagonists would cause vasodilation and worsen nasal congestion. β-adrenergic agonists act on bronchial rather than nasal vasculature. β-adrenergic antagonists do not relieve congestion and could worsen symptoms. Nicotinic cholinergic agents have no relevant role in nasal symptom control.
subject: Respiratory
concept_fingerprint: alpha agonist nasal congestion allergic rhinitis

text: A healthy 22-year-old man participates in a study that analyzes the effects of various therapies on gastrointestinal motility. A manometric tracing of this man is shown. This manometric pattern is most likely due to binding of which of the following neurotransmitters with its respective receptor in the stomach?
explanation: Gastric motility (peristaltic contractions) is primarily mediated by the release of acetylcholine (ACh) from enteric neurons (myenteric plexus). ACh binds to muscarinic M3 receptors on gastric smooth muscle cells, leading to depolarization, calcium influx, and contraction. The manometric tracing showing phasic contractions of the stomach in the fasting or fed state reflects these ACh-mediated contractions. Norepinephrine (via β-adrenergic receptors) inhibits gastric motility (relaxation). Vasoactive intestinal polypeptide (VIP) is an inhibitory neurotransmitter that causes smooth muscle relaxation. Serotonin (5-HT) modulates peristalsis via enteric neurons but ACh is the direct excitatory neurotransmitter. Motilin is a hormone (not a neurotransmitter) that induces phase III of the migrating motor complex (MMC), but the question explicitly asks about a neurotransmitter binding to its receptor.
subject: GI

text: A healthy 30-year-old woman is traveling on a commercial airliner where the cabin's barometric pressure is measured at 565 mm Hg. The inspiratory partial pressure of alveolar oxygen in this woman is most likely which of the following (in mm Hg)?
explanation: The alveolar gas equation calculates the partial pressure of oxygen in the alveoli (PAO2): PAO2 = PIO2 - (PaCO2 / R). First, calculate the inspired partial pressure of oxygen (PIO2): PIO2 = (Patm - PH2O) × FiO2 = (565 - 47) × 0.21 = 518 × 0.21 = 108.78 mm Hg. Assuming a normal PaCO2 of 40 mm Hg and a respiratory quotient (R) of 0.8: PAO2 = 108.78 - (40 / 0.8) = 108.78 - 50 = 58.78 ≈ 60 mm Hg. At this cabin pressure (equivalent to approximately 8,000 ft altitude), the PAO2 drops to about 60 mm Hg, which would cause mild hypoxemia but is generally well-tolerated in a healthy individual. 109 mm Hg would be approximately the PIO2. 27 mm Hg would be severely hypoxemic. 515 and 713 mm Hg are impossible at this atmospheric pressure.
subject: Respiratory

text: A 20-year-old man is brought to the physician by his mother because of bizarre behavior for 6 months. Although he had always been a good student, he failed all his classes at college last term. He no longer showers or shaves, and his appearance has become disheveled and unkempt. He appears distracted at the beginning of the interview and then begins talking nonstop to unseen people in the corner of the examining room. His mother looks upset and says, "It seems as if he's hearing voices all the time now. He's really scaring our family." Which of the following initial responses by the physician is most appropriate?

options.text: "He must be schizophrenic. Does schizophrenia run in your husband's family or yours?"
"He needs to take a shower. Have you tried sitting down with him and talking to him about taking better care of himself?"
"How frightening for you to see your son like this. Do you have any idea about what might be causing his behavior?"
"I am concerned he might be on drugs. Do you know anything about the friends he is hanging out with now?"
"Was he under any unusual stress at home or at school or did he have any problems with a girlfriend when all of this started?"

explanation: The most appropriate initial response is to acknowledge the mother's distress with empathy ("How frightening for you") and ask an open-ended question to gather more information. This validates the family's concerns without prematurely labeling the patient. Options A (immediately diagnosing schizophrenia) and D (assuming drug use) are premature and potentially stigmatizing. Option B dismisses the severity of the situation, and option E, while less harmful, focuses narrowly on stressors rather than the broader clinical picture of psychosis.
subject: Behavioral/Nervous & Special Senses

text: A 79-year-old woman comes to the physician because of swollen, painful joints in her hands and knees for 6 months. Her hematocrit is 39%. Serum protein electrophoresis shows a monoclonal IgG spike of 1.8 g; serum IgA and IgM concentrations are within the reference range. Her urine does not contain Bence Jones protein. A bone marrow biopsy specimen shows no abnormalities. Which of the following is the most likely explanation for the increased serum IgG concentration in this patient?
explanation:
Monoclonal gammopathy of uncertain significance (MGUS) is characterized by a serum monoclonal protein <3 g/dL, fewer than 10% bone marrow plasma cells, and no end-organ damage (e.g., lytic bone lesions, renal failure, hypercalcemia, anemia). This patient has a small IgG spike (1.8 g/dL) with normal IgA/IgM, no Bence Jones proteinuria, and a normal bone marrow biopsy, fitting MGUS. Multiple myeloma requires bone marrow plasmacytosis (≥10% plasma cells) and/or end-organ damage, which are absent. Waldenström macroglobulinemia produces an IgM monoclonal spike, not IgG. Chronic inflammation typically causes polyclonal, not monoclonal, hypergammaglobulinemia.

**Distractors:**
- **(A) Chronic hepatic disease:** Liver disease can cause polyclonal hypergammaglobulinemia and altered protein electrophoresis, but it does not produce an isolated monoclonal IgG spike.
- **(B) Chronic inflammation:** As noted, produces polyclonal gammopathy, not a monoclonal spike.
- **(D) Multiple myeloma:** Ruled out by normal bone marrow and absence of end-organ damage.
- **(E) Waldenström macroglobulinemia:** An IgM-secreting lymphoplasmacytic lymphoma; this patient has an IgG spike.
subject: Hemat/Lymph/Immune

text: In an experimental model of mild thermal injury to skin (a single application of 54°C for 20 seconds), the following pattern of extravasation of intravenously administered dye is observed. Administration of an antihistamine prior to thermal injury would have significantly blunted the extent of dye extravasation observed at which of the following labeled sites?
explanation:
Mild thermal injury produces a biphasic pattern of vascular extravasation. The early phase (Peak A, within minutes) is mediated primarily by histamine released from mast cells, and is significantly blunted by antihistamine pretreatment. The later phase (Peak B, hours later) is mediated by other inflammatory mediators including prostaglandins, leukotrienes, and bradykinin, which are not affected by antihistamines. Therefore, only the histamine-dependent Peak A would be significantly blunted.

**Distractors:**
- **B (Peak B only):** Incorrect because the late phase is driven by prostaglandins, leukotrienes, and bradykinin, not histamine.
- **C (Both peaks):** Incorrect because antihistamines do not inhibit late-phase mediators.
- **D (Neither peak):** Incorrect because the early phase is histamine-dependent and would be blunted by antihistamine pretreatment.
subject: General Principles

text: A 35-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department because of a 3-hour history of sharp cramping pain in the right flank. Urinalysis shows blood. A noncontrast CT scan is obtained and a renal calculus is found to be lodged in the ureter just above the sacroiliac joint. At this point, the ureter narrows as it passes over which of the following structures?
explanation:
The ureter has three anatomical points of narrowing: (1) the ureteropelvic junction, (2) where it crosses the pelvic brim over the external iliac vessels (at the sacroiliac joint level), and (3) the ureterovesical junction. A stone lodged just above the sacroiliac joint corresponds to the second narrowing, where the ureter passes anterior to the external iliac vessels as it enters the true pelvis.

**Distractors:**
- **B) Infundibulopelvic ligament:** While this ligament is near the ureter in the pelvis, it is not one of the three classic sites of ureteric narrowing.
- **C) Internal pudendal vessels:** These vessels are located in the perineum/pelvic floor and are not associated with the ureter at the sacroiliac joint.
- **D) Left colic vessels:** These are branches of the inferior mesenteric artery on the left side and are not related to the right ureter or its crossing at the pelvic brim.
- **E) Ovary:** The ovary lies in the lateral pelvic wall, but it is not a site of physiologic ureteric narrowing.
subject: Renal/Urinary

text: An inexpensive screening test for a disease is available through analysis of venous blood. The receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve for five different cut points is shown. The disease is irreversible and fatal if not discovered and treated early. Which of the following is the most appropriate cut point between normal and abnormal venous blood analysis results for this screening test?

options.text: curve for five different cut points is shown. The disease is irreversible and fatal if not discovered and treated early. Which of the following is the most appropriate cut point between normal and abnormal venous blood analysis results for this screening test?

explanation:
For an irreversible fatal disease where early treatment is critical, the screening test must maximize sensitivity (true positive rate) to avoid missing any cases, even at the cost of lower specificity (higher false positives). On an ROC curve, the cut point farthest to the left/upper-left corner provides the highest sensitivity. This corresponds to the lowest threshold for calling a test abnormal, ensuring that nearly all true cases are captured for early intervention.

Distractors: Cut points located toward the right/lower-right of the ROC curve favor specificity over sensitivity. While this reduces false positives and unnecessary follow-up testing, it would miss true cases of a fatal disease—an unacceptable outcome when early treatment is lifesaving. Intermediate points offer a trade-off that is inappropriate when the priority is detecting every possible case.
subject: General Principles

text: A 20-year-old man with intellectual disability is brought to the physician for a routine examination. Physical examination shows a long face, prominent ears, and large testes. His younger brother and a maternal uncle have similar features. Analysis of the patient's DNA shows 800 CGG repeated sequences (N<60) in the 5' untranslated region of the FMR1 gene. This region of expanded CGG trinucleotide repeats is heavily methylated. Which of the following is the most likely effect of these expanded nucleotide repeats on transcription of FMR1 mRNA?

options.text: Incorporation of CGG repeats into mRNA

explanation:
Fragile X syndrome is caused by >200 CGG repeats in the 5' UTR of FMR1. This expanded repeat becomes heavily methylated, leading to transcriptional silencing via heterochromatin formation. Decreased transcription of FMR1 results in loss of FMRP protein, which is essential for normal synaptic plasticity and dendritic spine maturation. The methylation of the expanded repeat silences the promoter, profoundly reducing mRNA transcription.

**Distractors:**
- **A) Alteration of mRNA splicing:** Splicing defects arise from mutations at splice sites or intronic/exonic boundaries, not from hypermethylation of a 5' UTR repeat.
- **C) Enhancement of mRNA degradation:** This describes post-transcriptional mechanisms such as nonsense-mediated decay; the primary defect in Fragile X is transcriptional silencing before mRNA is produced.
- **D) Incorporation of CGG repeats into mRNA:** Although the repeats lie in the 5' UTR and would be included in any transcript, the pathogenic mechanism here is not RNA toxicity from inclusion but rather the epigenetic blockade of transcription itself.
- **E) Increased binding of RNA polymerase:** Hypermethylation and heterochromatin formation decrease RNA polymerase access to the promoter, reducing—not increasing—transcription.
subject: Behavioral/Nervous & Special Senses

text: A 68-year-old man comes to the physician because of difficulty swallowing solids for 2 months. He has a history of dilated cardiomyopathy. X-rays of the esophagus with barium contrast show indentation and posterior displacement of the esophagus. Enlargement of which of the following structures is the most likely cause of the dysphagia?
explanation:
The esophagus descends through the posterior mediastinum directly anterior to the vertebral column and immediately posterior to the left atrium. Among the cardiac chambers, the left atrium is the most posterior and therefore lies in direct contact with the esophagus. In dilated cardiomyopathy, chronic volume and pressure overload lead to progressive left atrial enlargement, which can compress the adjacent esophagus and cause dysphagia. Barium swallow characteristically shows a smooth, extrinsic indentation with posterior displacement of the esophagus.

Distractors: The left ventricle (B) forms the apex and left lateral heart border but is not adjacent to the esophagus. The right atrium (C) and right ventricle (D) are anterior mediastinal structures and do not contact the esophagus. The superior vena cava (E) is located in the right superior mediastinum and does not course posteriorly enough to compress the esophagus.
subject: Cardiovascular

text: A 21-year-old man comes to the physician because of intermittent episodes of light brown urine during the past year associated with upper respiratory tract infections. His blood pressure is 145/85 mm Hg. Physical examination shows no other abnormalities. Urinalysis shows microscopic blood, 3+ protein, and several RBC casts. Immunohistochemical staining of a renal biopsy specimen is most likely to show granular deposits in the glomerular mesangium predominantly consisting of which of the following immunoglobulins?
explanation:
This presentation—episodic gross hematuria (light brown urine) following upper respiratory tract infections, hypertension, microscopic hematuria, proteinuria, and RBC casts—is classic for IgA nephropathy (Berger disease). IgA nephropathy is characterized by mesangial deposition of IgA-dominant immune complexes, identifiable by immunohistochemical staining. The granular mesangial deposits are predominantly IgA, differentiating it from other glomerulonephritides.

**Distractors:**
- **IgD:** Not a major participant in glomerular immune complex deposition.
- **IgE:** Mediates type I hypersensitivity and antiparasitic responses; not deposited in the glomerular mesangium.
- **IgM:** May be seen in other glomerulopathies (e.g., IgM nephropathy), but mesangial IgM is not the defining finding in this classic presentation.
subject: Renal/Urinary

text: For aerobic catabolism of compounds with equivalent numbers of carbon atoms, the greatest amount of energy in the form of ATP is obtained from compounds with the largest number of which of the following?
explanation:
In aerobic catabolism, ATP yield is proportional to the number of electrons available for transfer to the electron transport chain. Hydrogen atoms provide these electrons via NADH and FADH2 during beta-oxidation and the citric acid cycle. Compounds with more hydrogen atoms are more reduced and therefore yield more ATP when fully oxidized to CO2 and H2O. The more reduced a carbon compound is (i.e., more C-H bonds), the greater the energy yield upon complete oxidation.

**Distractors:** Aldehyde and keto groups represent more oxidized carbon states and thus contain fewer available electrons for the ETC. Amino groups are nitrogenous and must be removed before carbon skeletons enter catabolic pathways; they do not primarily determine ATP yield from carbon oxidation. Oxygen atoms indicate a more oxidized compound (e.g., carbohydrates vs fatty acids), which yields less ATP upon complete oxidation because fewer electrons are available to reduce NAD+ and FAD.
subject: General Principles

text: A 25-year-old man comes to the emergency department 5 hours after developing shortness of breath and chest pain during exercise; he has had no cough or bloody mucus. He has asthma and major depressive disorder. Current medications include fluticasone inhaler and albuterol. His temperature is 37.1°C ( 98.8°F), pulse is 110/min, respirations are 30/min, and blood pressure is 90/60 mm Hg. Pulse oximetry on room air shows an oxygen saturation of 93%. Cardiac examination shows a normal S₁ and S₂ with no murmurs and no increase in jugular venous pressure. Laboratory studies show: Hemoglobin 13 g/dL Hematocrit 39% Arterial blood gas analysis on room air: pH 7.46 PCO_₂ 26 mm Hg PO_₂ 60 mm Hg A chest x-ray is shown. Which of the following pulmonary findings are most likely in this patient?

options.text: Crackles on the left lung base and apex
Crackles on the right lung base
Decreased breath sounds on the left

explanation:
A young man with asthma who develops acute shortness of breath and chest pain during exercise, with hypotension, tachycardia, and hypoxia out of proportion to wheezing, most likely has a spontaneous pneumothorax. The chest x-ray would show a collapsed left lung with a pleural air collection. Physical exam findings consistent with pneumothorax include decreased breath sounds on the affected side (left), hyperresonance to percussion, and decreased tactile fremitus.

Distractors: Crackles (Options A and B) are typical of alveolar filling processes such as pneumonia or pulmonary edema, not pneumothorax. Increased wheezes on the left (Option D) would suggest bronchospasm from an asthma exacerbation, but this patient’s presentation with hypotension and marked hypoxia out of proportion to wheezing points toward pneumothorax rather than pure bronchospasm. Rhonchi on the right (Option E) indicate secretions in large airways and are not a feature of pneumothorax.
subject: Respiratory

text: A 42-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes mellitus comes to the physician because of a 1-day history of increasingly severe right knee pain. She now has difficulty walking because of the pain. She recalls no trauma to the knee and has never had similar symptoms. She is 152 cm (5 ft) tall and weighs 100 kg (220 lb); BMI is 43 kg/m². Her temperature is 39.3°C (102.7°F), pulse is 110/min, respirations are 12/min, and blood pressure is 160/90 mm Hg. Physical examination shows a 10-cm area of erythema surrounding the right knee, which is warm to the touch and exquisitely tender with movement. There is a moderate effusion. Arthrocentesis yields cloudy yellow synovial fluid. Analysis of the synovial fluid shows a leukocyte count of 90,000/mm³ (95% neutrophils) and no crystals. A Gram stain of the fluid shows numerous segmented neutrophils but no organisms. Which of the following is the most likely cause of the findings in this patient?

options.text: Deep venous thrombosis of the right common femoral vein

explanation:
**Correct answer: C. Infectious arthritis.** This patient has acute monoarticular septic arthritis involving the right knee, evidenced by high fever, marked erythema, warmth, severe pain with movement, and a moderate effusion. Synovial fluid analysis revealing 90,000 leukocytes/mm³ with 95% neutrophils is classic for a septic joint (>50,000/mm³). The Gram stain may be negative in a substantial proportion of cases due to fastidious organisms or prior antibiotic exposure, but this does not exclude the diagnosis. The absence of crystals makes gout and pseudogout unlikely. Urgent empiric antibiotics and surgical drainage are required to prevent irreversible cartilage destruction.

**Distractors:**
- **A. Deep venous thrombosis:** Would cause unilateral leg swelling and pain but not a warm, erythematous joint with purulent synovial fluid containing 90,000 WBC/mm³.
- **B. Gout:** Can present with acute monoarticular arthritis and low-grade fever, but synovial fluid analysis would demonstrate needle-shaped, negatively birefringent monosodium urate crystals.
- **D. Pseudogout:** Also causes acute crystal-induced monoarthritis, but synovial fluid would contain rhomboid, positively birefringent calcium pyrophosphate dihydrate crystals.
- **E. Ruptured Baker cyst:** Causes acute calf pain and swelling (pseudo-thrombophlebitis) but does not cause high fever, knee erythema, or septic synovial fluid.
subject: MSK/Skin

text: A 6-year-old girl of Mediterranean ancestry has severe anemia. Analysis shows normal production of α-globin gene mRNA. Production of β-globin gene mRNA is decreased 75% because of a splice-site mutation within both of the patient's β-globin genes. Which of the following is the most likely explanation for the anemia?

options.text: Decreased production of α-4 tetramers compared with normal individuals
Decreased production of β-4 tetramers compared with normal individuals
Imbalance in the synthesis of the α- and β-globin gene products
Imbalance in the synthesis of the four α-globin genes

explanation:
This patient has β-thalassemia major (Cooley anemia), caused by a splice-site mutation in both β-globin genes that reduces β-globin mRNA by 75%. Because α-globin synthesis is normal, the resulting imbalance between α- and β-globin chain production leads to excess free α-globin chains. These unpaired α chains precipitate in erythroid precursors, causing oxidative damage, ineffective erythropoiesis, and hemolytic anemia.

**Distractors:** Option A is incorrect because α4 tetramers are not relevant in β-thalassemia; excess α chains are unstable and precipitate rather than forming functional tetramers (β4 tetramers, or HbH, occur in α-thalassemia). Option B is incorrect because β chains are deficient, so β4 tetramers do not accumulate. Option D is incorrect because the four α-globin genes (two per haploid genome) are functioning normally; the problem is an imbalance between α- and β-globin gene products, not dysregulation among the α genes themselves.
subject: Hemat/Lymph/Immune

text: A 50-year-old man with schizophrenia is admitted to the hospital because of chest pain. He develops acute fever, lethargy, and muscular rigidity 5 days later. He has been receiving haloperidol treatment since admission. His temperature is 41°C (105.8°F), pulse is 120/min, and blood pressure is 140/80 mm Hg. He is disoriented and agitated and has diffusely increased muscle tone. Serum creatine kinase activity is 1500 U/L. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Neuroleptic malignant syndrome (NMS) is a life-threatening complication of antipsychotic medications like haloperidol. The classic tetrad includes fever (41°C), muscular rigidity, altered mental status (disorientation, agitation), and autonomic instability, with elevated creatine kinase from muscle breakdown.

**Distractors:** Catatonia can present with rigidity and mutism but typically lacks severe hyperthermia, autonomic instability, and markedly elevated CK; it is not specifically triggered by acute neuroleptic use. Dystonia presents as acute focal or generalized muscle spasm without fever, autonomic instability, or rhabdomyolysis. Malignant hyperthermia is triggered by volatile anesthetics or succinylcholine, not antipsychotics. Tardive dyskinesia is a chronic condition characterized by involuntary orofacial movements and does not present with fever, rigidity, or elevated CK.
subject: Behavioral/Nervous & Special Senses

text: A 1-month-old boy with X-linked severe combined immunodeficiency is enrolled in a gene therapy trial. Bone marrow stem cells are extracted from the patient and are treated ex vivo with a retrovirus expressing the wild-type gene. Although the patient initially responds well, 30 months after treatment he develops a form of T-lymphocyte leukemia. Molecular studies show that the T lymphocytes are monoclonal. Which of the following viral processes is the most likely cause of the leukemia in this patient?

options.text: Deactivation of the p53 tumor suppressor gene
Generation of the Philadelphia (Ph ¹) chromosome

explanation:
Retroviral gene therapy vectors integrate randomly into the host genome. In this case, the retrovirus integrated adjacent to a proto-oncogene (such as LMO2 in the well-known X-SCID gene therapy trial), leading to insertional mutagenesis and clonal T-lymphocyte proliferation. This is a recognized complication of retroviral vectors that lack insulator elements. The monoclonal T-cell population indicates that a single integration event drove leukemogenesis, consistent with oncogene activation.

**Distractors:** Deactivation of p53 (A) is characteristic of DNA tumor viruses (e.g., HPV E6), not retroviral insertional mutagenesis. The Philadelphia chromosome (B) arises from the t(9;22) translocation creating BCR-ABL in chronic myeloid leukemia and is unrelated to gene therapy vectors. Phosphorylation/inactivation of pRB (D) is mediated by DNA viral oncoproteins such as HPV E7. Reverse transcription of PTEN (E) is not a recognized leukemogenic mechanism; PTEN is a tumor suppressor, and retroviral reverse transcription is not gene-specific.
subject: Hemat/Lymph/Immune

text: A 72-year-old man with severe congestive heart failure is brought to the emergency department because of a 5-day history of malaise and vomiting. He takes no medications. His pulse is 104/min, respirations are 35/min, and blood pressure is 90/64 mm Hg. Physical examination shows dusky-colored skin, peripheral cyanosis, and 10-cm jugular venous distention. Crackles are heard over the lung bases bilaterally. Cardiac examination shows an S₃. There is 2+ pitting edema to the knees bilaterally. Laboratory studies show: Serum Na⁺ 127 mEq/L K⁺ 5.2 mEq/L Cl⁻ 79 mEq/L HCO₃⁻ 17 mEq/L Urea nitrogen 100 mg/dL Glucose 171 mg/dL Creatinine 8.4 mg/dL Urine Glucose 1+ Ketones absent Arterial blood gas analysis on 28% oxygen pH 7.35 PCO₂ 32 mm Hg PO₂ 154 mm Hg HCO₃⁻ 17 mEq/L ### Which of the following is the most likely cause of the anion gap in this patient?
explanation:
The anion gap is calculated as Na⁺ − (Cl⁻ + HCO₃⁻) = 127 − (79 + 17) = 31 mEq/L (elevated; normal ~8–12). The arterial blood gas shows a primary metabolic acidosis (low HCO₃⁻) with appropriate respiratory compensation (low PCO₂). This patient has acute-on-chronic renal failure (creatinine 8.4 mg/dL, BUN 100 mg/dL) secondary to severe CHF with cardiorenal syndrome. In renal failure, reduced clearance leads to accumulation of unmeasured anions—including phosphates, sulfates, urates, and organic acids—producing a high anion gap metabolic acidosis (uremic acidosis).

**Distractors:**
- **Alcoholic ketoacidosis (A)** and **diabetic ketoacidosis (B)** are incorrect because urine ketones are absent and the clinical picture is dominated by cardiorenal failure rather than alcohol use or DKA.
- **Hyperperfusion (C)** is incorrect; it does not produce an elevated anion gap.
- **Hypoalbuminemia (D)** typically lowers the anion gap because albumin is an unmeasured anion.
- **Metabolic alkalosis (E)** and **milk-alkali syndrome (F)** are incorrect because the patient is acidotic (pH 7.35, low HCO₃⁻), not alkalotic.
- **Respiratory alkalosis (H)** is present as compensation but is not the cause of the elevated anion gap; the anion gap reflects metabolic acids, not respiratory disorders.
subject: Renal/Urinary

text: A 24-year-old nulligravid woman comes to the office because of a 6-month history of chronic headache and vision difficulties. She also recently had several episodes of milky discharge from her breasts. Menses occur at irregular 50- to 90-day intervals; her last menstrual period was 6 months ago. She takes an oral contraceptive continuously and does not have withdrawal bleeding. Pulse is 80/min, respirations are 14/min, and blood pressure is 110/78 mm Hg. Ophthalmologic examination shows bitemporal hemianopia. Physical examination shows galactorrhea. Urine pregnancy test result is negative. MRI of the brain shows a 2-cm mass. Which of the following labeled structures in the normal MRI of the brain is the most likely location of the mass in this patient?
explanation:
The patient has amenorrhea, galactorrhea, bitemporal hemianopia, and irregular menses — classic for a pituitary adenoma (prolactinoma). Bitemporal hemianopia results from compression of the optic chiasm by a suprasellar mass. On MRI, a pituitary mass is located in the sella turcica, a depression in the sphenoid bone. Prolactinomas are the most common functional pituitary tumors and respond well to dopamine agonist therapy.

Distractors: The other labeled structures represent non-pituitary brain regions (e.g., cerebral cortex, ventricles, brainstem, cerebellum) that are not the site of prolactinomas and would not explain the combination of bitemporal hemianopia with galactorrhea and amenorrhea.
subject: Reproductive/Endocrine

text: Diisopropyl fluorophosphate, a potent inhibitor of acetylcholinesterase, reacts with which of the following specific amino acids at the active site of the enzyme?
explanation:
Diisopropyl fluorophosphate (DFP) is an organophosphate that irreversibly inhibits acetylcholinesterase by phosphorylating the active-site serine hydroxyl group. Organophosphates form a covalent bond with the serine residue at the catalytic triad (Ser-His-Glu) of acetylcholinesterase, rendering the enzyme permanently inactive. This is the same mechanism by which other organophosphates (e.g., sarin, malathion) exert their toxic effects through cholinergic excess.

**Distractors:** Cysteine is the key nucleophile in thiol-dependent enzymes and cysteine proteases, but it is not the residue phosphorylated by organophosphates. Glutamic acid and histidine are components of the catalytic triad that facilitate serine activation, yet they are not themselves covalently modified by DFP. Tyrosine hydroxyl groups are phosphorylated by kinases in cell signaling, but tyrosine is not the target residue in acetylcholinesterase inhibition.
subject: General Principles

text: ☐A) ☐B) ☐C) ☐D) ☐E) ☐F) ☐G) ☐H) ☐I) ☐J) 18. Following a stroke, a 68-year-old man has a language problem. His speech is fluent but contains many grammatical errors, word substitutions, and neologisms. He is unable to repeat words after the examiner and is apparently unable to comprehend other verbal requests. Which of the following labeled sites on the photograph of the left hemisphere is most likely to be damaged?

options.text: ☐B) ☐C) ☐D) ☐E) ☐F) ☐G) ☐H) ☐I) ☐J) 18. Following a stroke, a 68-year-old man has a language problem. His speech is fluent but contains many grammatical errors, word substitutions, and neologisms. He is unable to repeat words after the examiner and is apparently unable to comprehend other verbal requests. Which of the following labeled sites on the photograph of the left hemisphere is most likely to be damaged?

explanation:
This patient has fluent (Wernicke) aphasia, characterized by fluent speech with paraphasic errors (word substitutions), neologisms (made-up words), poor comprehension, and poor repetition. The responsible lesion is in Wernicke's area in the posterior superior temporal gyrus of the dominant (left) hemisphere. This is distinct from Broca aphasia (non-fluent, preserved comprehension), conduction aphasia (poor repetition, fluent), and transcortical aphasias (preserved repetition).

Distractors: Other labeled sites likely correspond to Broca area (inferior frontal gyrus), which produces nonfluent aphasia with preserved comprehension and is therefore inconsistent with this patient’s fluent speech and poor comprehension. A lesion of the arcuate fasciculus causes conduction aphasia with fluent speech and poor repetition but relatively preserved comprehension, which also does not fit. Transcortical aphasias spare repetition, unlike this patient. Other cortical regions (e.g., primary motor or sensory cortex) would cause focal motor or sensory deficits rather than a fluent aphasic syndrome.
subject: Behavioral/Nervous & Special Senses

text: A male newborn develops vomiting and convulsions 4 hours after delivery. There is slight bulging of the fontanelles. Which of the following organisms is most likely responsible for these findings?
explanation:
Early-onset neonatal meningitis (within the first week of life) is most commonly caused by Group B *Streptococcus* (*Streptococcus agalactiae*) or *Escherichia coli*. Among the options given, *E. coli* is the most common gram-negative cause of neonatal meningitis. Newborns present with nonspecific signs including vomiting, seizures (convulsions), and bulging fontanelles due to increased intracranial pressure from meningeal inflammation. The timing of 4 hours after delivery points to vertically transmitted early-onset infection.

**Distractors:**
- **B. *Haemophilus influenzae***: Classically causes meningitis in unvaccinated children aged 6 months to 6 years; it is not a typical pathogen in the immediate neonatal period.
- **C. *Neisseria meningitidis***: Most common in adolescents and young adults (epidemic/closed populations); rare in neonates.
- **D. *Staphylococcus aureus***: An uncommon cause of neonatal meningitis unless associated with trauma, neurosurgery, or indwelling devices.
- **E. *Streptococcus pneumoniae***: A leading cause of meningitis in adults and children >3 months, but not characteristic of early-onset neonatal disease.
subject: Behavioral/Nervous & Special Senses

text: A 23-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a 2-week history of increasingly severe itching and yellow-tinged skin. Three months ago, she started taking a combination oral contraceptive. She does not smoke. She consumes two to three alcoholic beverages only on the weekends. Physical examination shows mild jaundice and scleral icterus. The liver span is 11 cm with no tenderness. Serum studies show: Bilirubin, total 7.3 mg/dL Direct 5.8 mg/dL Alkaline phosphatase 440 U/L AST 80 U/L ALT 70 U/L γ-Glutamyltransferase (GGT) 234 U/L (N=0-30) Serologic studies for acute viral hepatitis are negative. Which of the following is the most likely cause of these findings?
explanation:
Oral contraceptives can cause intrahepatic cholestasis in susceptible individuals, presenting with jaundice, pruritus, and a cholestatic liver enzyme pattern (markedly elevated alkaline phosphatase and GGT with only mild transaminitis). The pathophysiology involves estrogen-induced impairment of bile salt transporters, leading to dilated canaliculi with bile plugs (cholestasis). The negative viral hepatitis serologies rule out acute hepatitis, and the pattern is not hemolytic or ischemic.

**Distractors:**
- **Autoimmune hemolytic anemia (A)** would produce unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia with elevated LDH and reticulocytosis, not a cholestatic pattern with elevated direct bilirubin, alkaline phosphatase, and GGT.
- **Hepatic vein thrombosis/Budd-Chiari (C)** typically presents with acute painful hepatomegaly, ascites, and markedly elevated transaminases from hepatic congestion and ischemic necrosis rather than a predominant cholestatic picture.
- **Hepatocellular necrosis (D)** is seen in acute viral or toxic hepatitis and produces markedly elevated AST/ALT (often >10× upper limit of normal) with only modest rises in alkaline phosphatase, which contradicts this patient's laboratory profile.
- **Portal vein thrombosis (E)** usually manifests with signs of portal hypertension (ascites, splenomegaly, varices) and typically does not cause isolated cholestatic jaundice with such pronounced alkaline phosphatase and GGT elevation.
subject: GI

text: A 17-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department because of a 2-day history of fever and shortness of breath. He underwent bone marrow transplantation for acute myelogenous leukemia 2 months ago. His temperature is 39°C (102.2°F), and respirations are 32/min. Diffuse crackles are heard over the lung fields on auscultation. A chest x-ray shows interstitial pneumonia. A photomicrograph of a biopsy specimen of the lung tissue is shown. Decreased function of which of the following most likely predisposed this patient to infection?
explanation:
Two months after bone marrow transplantation, the patient's T lymphocytes are still functionally deficient while other immune cells (neutrophils, dendritic cells, mast cells) may have recovered. This T-cell deficiency predisposes to opportunistic infections with intracellular pathogens, particularly CMV (a common cause of interstitial pneumonia in BMT recipients) and Pneumocystis jirovecii. The photomicrograph likely shows characteristic viral inclusions or Pneumocystis organisms.

Distractors: Neutrophils typically engraft and recover within 2–4 weeks after BMT, so by 2 months they are functional and not the primary defect. Dendritic cells generally recover earlier than T cells and are not the principal determinant of susceptibility to CMV/PJP in this timeframe. Mast cells are tissue-resident and not a major factor in post-transplant opportunistic pneumonia. Eosinophils are involved in allergic responses and parasitic infections, not the viral/opportunistic pathogens seen in T-cell deficiency.
subject: Hemat/Lymph/Immune

text: Which of the following curves shows the highest cooperativity between a hormone and its receptor?
explanation:
Cooperativity refers to the phenomenon where binding of one ligand molecule to a receptor changes the affinity for subsequent ligand molecules. Positive cooperativity produces a sigmoidal binding curve (S-shaped) on a plot of fractional saturation vs. ligand concentration. The most sigmoidal curve among the options indicates the highest degree of positive cooperativity, which facilitates an ultrasensitive response to small changes in hormone concentration.

**Distractors:** The other curves likely show less sigmoidal or hyperbolic binding kinetics, indicating independent binding sites without cooperativity, or lower degrees of positive cooperativity. Hyperbolic curves are characteristic of simple mass-action binding without cooperative interactions, and any curve that deviates less from hyperbolic shape reflects weaker cooperativity.
subject: General Principles

text: A 17-year-old girl with type 1 diabetes mellitus comes to the physician for a follow-up examination. She has had multiple admissions to the hospital during the past 5 months for diabetic ketoacidosis. She appears well. Physical examination shows no abnormalities. Laboratory studies show a hemoglobin A₁c of 11.5%. She tells the physician that she does not take her insulin regularly because she either forgets to or is too busy. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial step by the physician?

options.text: Acknowledge the patient's reasons for missing insulin injections
Discuss the patient's noncompliance with her parents
Educate the patient about the long-term complications of untreated diabetes
Tell the patient's parents to ensure that their daughter is compliant
Refer the patient to a psychologist

explanation:
The most appropriate initial step is to acknowledge the patient's stated reasons for missing insulin injections (forgetting or being too busy). This uses motivational interviewing techniques and builds therapeutic alliance, validating the patient's perspective rather than confronting or judging her.

**Why the distractors are incorrect:**
- **B & D:** Involving the parents without the patient's consent undermines adolescent autonomy and damages the therapeutic relationship.
- **C:** Prematurely discussing long-term complications may increase patient resistance and is less effective before establishing rapport.
- **E:** Referral to a psychologist is premature before first understanding the patient's barriers through direct rapport-building.
subject: Behavioral/Nervous & Special Senses

text: A 63-year-old man from southern China has had a bloody nasal discharge for the past 5 months. Physical examination shows an enlarged, fixed lymph node in the upper posterior cervical triangle of the left neck. Examination of tissue obtained on needle biopsy of the lymph node shows neoplastic cells that are positive for keratin and Epstein-Barr nuclear antigen. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Nasopharyngeal carcinoma (NPC) is strongly associated with Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) and has a high incidence in southern Chinese populations. Keratin positivity indicates epithelial origin (carcinoma), and EBNA (Epstein-Barr nuclear antigen) positivity confirms EBV association. The classic presentation includes epistaxis (bloody nasal discharge) and a fixed cervical lymph node, often in the posterior cervical triangle. This combination is highly specific for NPC.

Distractors: Burkitt lymphoma (A) is also EBV-associated but is a B-cell lymphoma that would be keratin-negative and typically presents with jaw or abdominal disease rather than epistaxis. Kaposi sarcoma (B) is a mesenchymal vascular tumor driven by HHV-8 (not EBV) and would be keratin-negative. Sinonasal carcinoma (D) is epithelial and keratin-positive but lacks the strong EBV association and epidemiologic predilection seen in NPC. Squamous cell carcinoma (E) of the head and neck is keratin-positive but is typically associated with tobacco and alcohol use, not EBV, and does not share the same endemic epidemiology; while NPC is technically a subtype of squamous cell carcinoma, the distinct EBV-positive entity is the intended diagnosis.
subject: Respiratory

text: A 55-year-old man comes to the physician because of pain and stiffness of his right hand and wrist for 3 months. The pain is exacerbated by hand movement and is relieved by rest. He was a professional boxer for 15 years. Physical examination shows moderate swelling over the dorsum of the right wrist. Examination of fluid aspirated from the wrist shows: Appearance Leukocyte count Neutrophils Glucose Clear, yellowish 250/mm³ (N≤200) 5% (N≤25%) 101 mg/dL (N=80–100) Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's condition?
explanation:
This patient has osteoarthritis, likely secondary to his history as a professional boxer causing repetitive microtrauma to the wrist. The synovial fluid is clear and yellowish with a normal leukocyte count (250/mm³), low neutrophil percentage (5%), and normal glucose — consistent with a non-inflammatory (mechanical/degenerative) process. This rules out gout (inflammatory, crystals), septic arthritis (markedly elevated WBC, low glucose), and rheumatoid arthritis (inflammatory).

**Distractors:**
- **Acute gouty arthritis:** Would present with inflammatory synovial fluid (elevated WBC, neutrophils >70%) and negatively birefringent needle-shaped crystals.
- **Rheumatoid arthritis:** Would show inflammatory synovial fluid (WBC 2000–50,000/mm³, neutrophils >50%) due to autoimmune synovitis; glucose may be low.
- **Septic arthritis:** Would show markedly elevated WBC (>50,000/mm³, neutrophils >75%), purulent/cloudy fluid, and low glucose due to bacterial consumption.
- **Normal age-related changes:** Would not cause moderate swelling, chronic pain exacerbated by movement, or synovial fluid leukocytosis; osteoarthritis is a pathologic degenerative process rather than normal aging.
subject: MSK/Skin

text: A 34-year-old woman has a 3-year history of recurring episodes of tenesmus, mucoid bloody diarrhea, and cramping abdominal pain. A section of bowel removed following a severe episode is shown. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Recurrent episodes of tenesmus, mucoid bloody diarrhea, and cramping abdominal pain are classic for ulcerative colitis (UC). UC is a chronic inflammatory bowel disease confined to the colorectal mucosa, typically involving the rectum and extending proximally in a continuous fashion. The bowel section shown likely demonstrates characteristic superficial mucosal inflammation, crypt abscesses, and loss of haustrations — distinguishing it from Crohn disease (transmural, skip lesions, granulomas).

Distractors:
- A) Crohn disease: typically causes transmural inflammation with skip lesions, nonbloody diarrhea, and granulomas; it is not limited to the mucosa and often involves the small bowel.
- B) Diverticulitis: acute inflammation of colonic diverticula, usually in older adults; presents with left lower quadrant pain and fever, not a chronic 3-year history of tenesmus and mucoid bloody diarrhea.
- C) Pseudomembranous enterocolitis: caused by Clostridioides difficile toxin, usually following antibiotic exposure; presents acutely with watery diarrhea and pseudomembranes, not a chronic relapsing course.
- D) Superior mesenteric artery occlusion: causes acute mesenteric ischemia with sudden severe abdominal pain and bloody diarrhea; it is a vascular emergency, not a chronic inflammatory condition.
subject: GI

text: A 22-year-old woman is admitted to the hospital because of a 10-day history of polydipsia and polyuria. She says that the urge to urinate often awakens her at night. She has been taking lithium carbonate for 2 years for bipolar disorder; her dosage was increased 6 months ago because of recurrent severe manic episodes. Her vital signs are within normal limits. Physical examination shows no abnormalities. Over the next 24 hours, urine excretion totals 6.5 L. Laboratory studies at this time show a serum sodium concentration of 148 mEq/L, serum osmolality of 315 mOsm/kg, and urine osmolality of 75 mOsm/kg. After administration of desmopressin, urine output and osmolality do not change. Which of the following findings in the nephron best describes the tubular osmolality, compared with serum, in this patient? Proximal Tubule Juxtaglomerular Apparatus Medullary Collecting Duct A) Hypertonic hypertonic hypertonic B) Hypertonic hypertonic hypotonic C) Hypertonic hypotonic hypotonic D) Isotonic isotonic isotonic E) Isotonic isotonic isotonic F) Isotonic isotonic isotonic G) Hypotonic hypotonic hypotonic H) Hypotonic hypotonic hypotonic I) Hypotonic hypotonic hypotonic
explanation: Lithium causes nephrogenic diabetes insipidus (NDI) by downregulating aquaporin-2 water channels in the collecting duct, making it resistant to ADH (desmopressin). In NDI: the proximal tubule reabsorbs isotonically (hypertonic to serum relative to the table's phrasing? Actually the proximal tubule is isotonic in all conditions), the thick ascending limb/JGA area creates a hypotonic fluid (diluting segment), and the medullary collecting duct remains hypotonic because ADH cannot facilitate water reabsorption. The absence of response to desmopressin confirms a nephrogenic (not central) DI.
subject: NBME 29

text: A 58-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes mellitus is brought to the emergency department because of an 18-hour history of fever, confusion, and pain of her left leg. Her temperature is 39.6°C ( 103.3°F), pulse is 124/min, respirations are 22/min, and blood pressure is 94/60 mm Hg. Physical examination shows a diffuse, erythematous rash and conjunctival injection. Erythema and edema extend from the dorsum of the left foot to the knee. She is oriented to person but not to place or time. Neurologic examination shows no other abnormalities. Serum studies show: Urea nitrogen 36 mg/dL Creatinine 2.8 mg/dL Total bilirubin 2.2 mg/dL AST 470 U/L ALT 385 U/L One day later, blood cultures grow gram-positive cocci in chains. These bacteria most likely produced a toxin that caused this patient's condition via which of the following mechanisms?

options.text: Binding to the T-lymphocyte receptor and class II MHC molecules
Blockade of protein synthesis by depurination of ribosomal RNA
Catalyzing of the formation of cAMP from ATP
Cleavage of kinases that activate mitogen-activated protein kinase to induce macrophage apoptosis
Disruption of cytoskeleton architecture by glycosylating Rho1

explanation:
Group A Streptococcus (Streptococcus pyogenes), which grows as gram-positive cocci in chains, produces superantigen exotoxins (SpeA, SpeC, SSA) that cause streptococcal toxic shock syndrome (STSS). These superantigens bind directly to the T-cell receptor Vβ domain and class II MHC molecules on antigen-presenting cells, bypassing normal antigen processing and causing massive T-cell activation and cytokine storm (TNF-α, IL-1, IL-6). This produces fever, hypotension, multi-organ failure, and diffuse erythematous rash.

Distractors:
- B) Blockade of protein synthesis by depurination of ribosomal RNA describes Shiga toxin (produced by Shigella dysenteriae and EHEC) and ricin, which inhibit protein synthesis by depurinating 28S rRNA.
- C) Catalyzing the formation of cAMP from ATP describes anthrax edema factor (direct adenylate cyclase) and cholera toxin (indirectly via ADP-ribosylation of Gs), neither of which is a streptococcal superantigen.
- D) Cleavage of kinases that activate mitogen-activated protein kinase to induce macrophage apoptosis describes anthrax lethal factor, a zinc metalloprotease that cleaves MAPKKs, not a GAS toxin.
- E) Disruption of cytoskeleton architecture by glycosylating Rho1 describes Clostridioides difficile toxin B, which glucosylates Rho GTPases to cause actin depolymerization and pseudomembranous colitis.
subject: Multisystem

text: A newborn born with ambiguous external genitalia becomes severely dehydrated shortly after birth. Serum sodium and chloride concentrations are decreased, and serum potassium concentration is increased. The newborn's karyotype is 46,XX. The most likely cause of these findings is a genetic defect in which of the following labeled enzymes?

options.text: The most likely cause of these findings is a genetic defect in which of the following labeled enzymes?

explanation:
A 46,XX newborn with ambiguous genitalia (virilized female), severe dehydration, hyponatremia, hyperkalemia, and volume depletion has salt-wasting congenital adrenal hyperplasia (CAH) due to 21-hydroxylase deficiency. The enzyme defect blocks conversion of 17-hydroxyprogesterone to 11-deoxycortisol and progesterone to 11-deoxycorticosterone, preventing cortisol and aldosterone synthesis. Loss of cortisol negative feedback increases ACTH, causing adrenal hyperplasia and shunting of accumulated precursors into the androgen pathway; excess androgens virilize the 46,XX fetus. Cortisol deficiency produces hypotension and impaired stress response, while aldosterone deficiency causes renal salt wasting, hyponatremia, hyperkalemia, and hypovolemia.

Distractors: Other enzymes commonly labeled in adrenal steroidogenesis diagrams do not fit this phenotype. 17α-hydroxylase/17,20-lyase deficiency causes hypertension and hypokalemia (due to accumulated mineralocorticoid precursors), and 46,XX individuals have normal female genitalia. 11β-hydroxylase deficiency causes virilization but also hypertension from excess deoxycorticosterone (DOC). 3β-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase deficiency can cause salt-wasting but does not produce marked virilization in 46,XX because the enzymatic block precedes active androgen synthesis. Cholesterol desmolase deficiency causes severe salt-wasting but is rare and typically associated with 46,XY undervirilization.
subject: Reproductive/Endocrine

text: A 25-year-old man comes to the physician because of a 2-month history of recurrent episodes of chest pain and shortness of breath. He has a 2-year history of nodules on his hands and feet. Physical examination shows numerous 1- to 2-cm yellow nodules that are palpable on both Achilles tendons and on the extensor tendons of the hands. Ophthalmologic examination shows corneal arcus. Serum studies show: Creatine kinase Cholesterol, total Triglycerides Troponin I 100 mg/dL 0.1 ng/mL (N<0.4) An ECG shows no abnormalities. This patient most likely has an impairment in function involving which of the following structures?
explanation:
This patient has familial hypercholesterolemia (FH), evidenced by tendon xanthomas on the Achilles and extensor tendons, corneal arcus, and markedly elevated cholesterol. FH is most commonly caused by defective LDL receptor function, which impairs receptor-mediated endocytosis via clathrin-coated pits. LDL receptors normally cluster in clathrin-coated pits on the cell surface to internalize LDL particles; dysfunctional receptors cannot be properly internalized, leading to elevated serum LDL cholesterol and premature atherosclerosis.

Distractors:
- **A. Caveolae**: Caveolae are flask-shaped invaginations involved in transcytosis and some lipid trafficking, but they are not the primary route for LDL receptor internalization.
- **C. COPII-coated pit**: COPII-coated vesicles mediate anterograde transport from the endoplasmic reticulum to the Golgi apparatus; they are not involved in endocytosis at the plasma membrane.
- **D. Phagosome**: Phagosomes are formed during phagocytosis to engulf large particles or microbes; they are not involved in receptor-mediated endocytosis of LDL.
- **E. SNAREs**: SNARE proteins mediate the fusion of vesicles with target membranes (e.g., synaptic vesicle exocytosis), not the initial internalization of receptors into coated pits.
subject: General Principles

text: Patients who have recurrent infections involving Neisseria species are most likely to have a genetic deficiency in which of the following serum factors?
explanation:
Recurrent Neisseria (meningitidis and gonorrhoeae) infections are the hallmark of late complement component deficiencies (C5–C9, the membrane attack complex). The terminal complement pathway (MAC) is essential for killing Neisseria species via serum bactericidal activity. Deficiencies in early components (C1–C4) more often present with autoimmune disease (SLE-like syndromes). C1 esterase inhibitor deficiency causes hereditary angioedema, and factors B and H deficiencies cause atypical HUS.

Distractors:
- Immunoglobulins: Deficiency causes recurrent sinopulmonary and encapsulated bacterial infections (e.g., Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae), not specifically recurrent Neisseria.
- β₂-Microglobulin: A structural component of MHC class I molecules; deficiency is not associated with recurrent Neisseria infections.
subject: Hemat/Lymph/Immune

text: A 17-year-old boy comes to the physician because of a 3-month history of worsening acne. Treatment over the past year with tetracycline had been effective. His symptoms began when he started taking the medication in the morning with a glass of milk. Which of the following best explains the ineffectiveness of tetracycline in this patient?
explanation:
Tetracycline chelates divalent and trivalent cations, particularly calcium, forming an insoluble complex that cannot be absorbed from the gastrointestinal tract. When taken with milk (rich in calcium), the drug's bioavailability is significantly reduced, rendering it ineffective. This is why tetracycline should be taken on an empty stomach or at least 2 hours apart from dairy products, antacids, or iron supplements.

**Distractors:**
- **B:** Milk does not contain carbonate that inactivates tetracycline; the interaction is specifically cation chelation, not chemical inactivation by carbonate.
- **C:** Milk lipids do not significantly bind tetracycline; calcium chelation is the principal mechanism reducing absorption.
- **D:** Milk peptides do not induce drug-metabolizing enzymes (e.g., CYP450); the ineffectiveness is due to impaired absorption, not increased metabolism.
- **E:** Although proteins can bind some drugs, milk proteins are not the major cause of reduced tetracycline bioavailability; calcium chelation is the established interaction.
subject: General Principles

text: A 50-year-old woman has azotemia. Renal ultrasonography shows bilateral hydroureters and hydronephrosis. The most likely cause of these findings is primary carcinoma of which of the following?
explanation:
Bilateral hydroureter and hydronephrosis indicate bilateral ureteral obstruction, most commonly at the level of the bladder trigone or distal ureters. Advanced carcinoma of the uterine cervix can directly invade the posterior bladder wall and trigone, compressing or obstructing both ureteral orifices. This is a classic complication of locally invasive cervical cancer and can lead to postrenal azotemia.

Distractors:
- **A. Colon:** Colorectal carcinoma may invade a ureter locally but typically causes unilateral obstruction or luminal bowel obstruction; it does not characteristically infiltrate the bladder trigone to cause bilateral distal ureteral obstruction.
- **B. Kidney:** Renal cell carcinoma arises from the kidney parenchyma and usually presents with hematuria, flank pain, or a renal mass; it does not typically cause bilateral hydroureter/hydronephrosis from a single primary lesion.
- **C. Ovary:** Ovarian carcinoma most commonly spreads by peritoneal seeding, producing ascites and omental metastases. While bulky disease can compress ureters, bilateral distal obstruction via trigone invasion is not characteristic.
- **D. Ureter:** Primary ureteral carcinoma (urothelial carcinoma) is uncommon and would generally cause unilateral—not bilateral—ureteral obstruction and hydronephrosis.
subject: Reproductive/Endocrine

text: A 45-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department because of the sudden onset of severe abdominal pain. Examination shows an irregularly irregular pulse, a grade 3/6, apical diastolic murmur, and an opening snap. An x-ray of the abdomen shows distention of the small intestine, the ascending colon, and a portion of the transverse colon. Which of the following is the most likely underlying cause of these findings?
explanation:
This patient has atrial fibrillation (irregularly irregular pulse) and mitral stenosis (apical diastolic murmur with opening snap). The abdominal findings (distended small intestine, ascending and proximal transverse colon) suggest acute superior mesenteric artery (SMA) occlusion. Embolization from a left atrial thrombus (due to mitral stenosis and AFib) is the most likely cause. The SMA distribution explains the pattern up to the transverse colon (splenic flexure watershed).

Distractors: Atherosclerosis typically causes chronic mesenteric ischemia or local thrombosis rather than acute embolic occlusion, and it does not explain the cardiac findings. Hemorrhage would present with bleeding signs, not isolated bowel distention from ischemia. Plaque rupture is associated with coronary or cerebrovascular thrombosis, not systemic emboli to the SMA. Thrombosis in situ can occur but is less likely than embolization given the clear cardiac source of stasis (mitral stenosis with atrial fibrillation).
subject: GI
concept_fingerprint: SMA embolization from mitral stenosis AFib

text: A 67-year-old man comes to the physician because of a 2-month history of pain in his feet. The discomfort is more severe in bed at night and is relieved by taking a hot bath. He has type 2 diabetes mellitus treated with lipozide. His pulse is 60/min, respirations are 12/min, and blood pressure is 130/88 mm Hg. Strength is normal and symmetric in the distal and proximal upper and lower extremities. The Achilles deep tendon reflexes are decreased, and quadriceps deep tendon reflexes are normal. Sensation to pinprick and vibration is decreased from just above the ankles distally. This patient is most likely to describe his pain as which of the following?
explanation:
Diabetic peripheral neuropathy typically presents with symmetric, length-dependent sensory loss, diminished distal reflexes, and pain described as 'burning,' 'tingling,' or 'pins and needles' (neuropathic pain). The decreased pinprick and vibration sensation from the ankles distally confirms a stocking-glove polyneuropathy. Neuropathic pain in diabetes is characteristically described as burning rather than aching (musculoskeletal), sharp (acute injury), cramping (vascular), or squeezing (angina).

**Distractors:** Colicky pain is characteristic of hollow viscus obstruction (e.g., renal colic, biliary colic, intestinal colic).
subject: Behavioral/Nervous & Special Senses

text: A 35-year-old woman comes to the physician for advice on smoking cessation. She has smoked 2 packs of cigarettes daily for 15 years. She has tried to quit smoking numerous times in the past without success. The physician plans to prescribe a medication that decreases the craving for cigarettes and also blocks the central nervous system stimulation caused by smoking. This drug most likely has which of the following nicotinic effects?
explanation:
Varenicline is a partial agonist at α4β2 nicotinic acetylcholine receptors — it provides moderate agonist activity (reducing cravings and withdrawal symptoms) while simultaneously blocking the full stimulatory effect of nicotine from cigarettes. A pure antagonist would block nicotine's effects but not reduce cravings. A full agonist would produce overstimulation. The partial agonist profile provides the optimal balance for smoking cessation by reducing both craving and reward from smoking.

Distractors: A full agonist (choice A) would cause continuous receptor overstimulation and would not competitively block nicotine's rewarding CNS effects. A pure antagonist (choice B) would prevent nicotine binding but lacks the moderate agonist activity required to suppress cravings and withdrawal. An inverse agonist (choice C) would suppress constitutive receptor activity below baseline, which does not describe varenicline's mechanism and would not provide the desired clinical effect.
subject: General Principles

text: A 35-year-old man comes to the physician because of a 2-week history of daily left-sided headaches that last 30 to 60 minutes. The headaches usually occur at night and often awaken him. They are accompanied by redness and tearing of the left eye and nasal congestion on the left. Alcohol seems to trigger their occurrence. Vital signs are normal. Neurologic examination shows no abnormalities. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Cluster headache is characterized by unilateral, severe, short-duration (15–180 minutes) headaches with ipsilateral autonomic features (conjunctival injection, lacrimation, nasal congestion, rhinorrhea). The nocturnal occurrence, alcohol triggering, and circadian periodicity are classic.

Distractors: Alcohol-induced vasodilation (A) is a physiologic trigger but not a recognized headache diagnosis. Allergic rhinitis (B) causes bilateral nasal congestion and sneezing without severe unilateral periorbital pain or nocturnal timing. Central nervous system neoplasia (C) typically produces progressive headaches, focal neurologic deficits, or papilledema, none of which are present here. Temporal arteritis (E) occurs in patients older than 50 years and is associated with jaw claudication, elevated ESR, and vision changes rather than autonomic tearing and nasal congestion.
subject: Behavioral/Nervous & Special Senses
concept_fingerprint: Cluster headache unilateral autonomic alcohol nocturnal

text: A 4-year-old girl with chronic otitis media is brought to the physician by her mother because of a 5-day history of recurrence of symptoms. The mother says that her daughter had a mild cough that began 8 days ago and progressed to a sore throat and ear pain during the next 3 days. The patient appears irritable and is pulling at her right ear. Otosopic examination shows fluid behind the tympanic membrane. Which of the following best describes the anatomic pathway of the spread of infection from this patient's throat?

options.text: Larynx → oropharynx → sinuses → inner and middle ear

explanation:
Acute otitis media in children typically results from infection spreading from the nasopharynx to the middle ear via the auditory (Eustachian) tube. The auditory tube connects the nasopharynx to the middle ear cavity and normally drains middle ear secretions. In children, the tube is shorter and more horizontal, making reflux of nasopharyngeal pathogens (*Streptococcus pneumoniae*, *Haemophilus influenzae*, *Moraxella catarrhalis*) into the middle ear more likely.

**Distractors:**
- **A:** Incorrect because the auditory tube opens into the **nasopharynx**, not the laryngopharynx, and acute otitis media involves the **middle ear**, not the inner ear.
- **B:** Incorrect because the larynx is not the origin of spread to the ear, and the inner ear is not the primary site of infection in acute otitis media.
- **C:** Incorrect because the lungs are not the source of spread in this scenario, and the inner ear is not involved.
- **E:** Incorrect because acute otitis media affects the **middle ear**, not the outer ear, and the paranasal sinuses are not the direct conduit.
subject: Behavioral/Nervous & Special Senses
concept_fingerprint: Eustachian tube nasopharynx middle ear anatomy

text: An investigator is conducting a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled clinical trial of a new medication for the treatment of mild insomnia in adults. A total of 2000 participants are enrolled in the study and randomized to one of two groups: 1000 participants receive the new medication (Group 1), and 1000 participants receive a placebo that appears identical to the medication (Group 2). Participants in both groups are instructed to take one pill 30 minutes before bedtime each day and to keep a sleep diary. After 1 month, each participant is interviewed, and the daily sleep diaries are reviewed. At follow-up, it is determined that 200 participants in Group 1 and 50 participants in Group 2 did not take the pill as directed. In accordance with intention-to-treat analysis, how should the data pertaining to all individuals who did not adhere to the instructions be treated?

options.text: Analyze all nonadherent participants according to the group of the study to which each was randomized
Exclude all nonadherent participants from analysis
Exclude only nonadherent participants in Group 1 from analysis
Exclude only nonadherent participants in Group 2 from analysis
Perform separate analyses of the 250 nonadherent participants and the 1750 adherent participants

explanation:
Intention-to-treat (ITT) analysis requires that all participants be analyzed according to the group to which they were originally randomized, regardless of whether they completed the protocol or adhered to treatment. This preserves the benefits of randomization (balancing confounders between groups) and prevents bias from differential dropout. Analyzing nonadherent participants by their randomized group provides a pragmatic estimate of real-world treatment effect.

Distractors:
- **B (Exclude all nonadherent):** This describes a per-protocol or as-treated analysis. Excluding nonadherent participants breaks randomization and introduces selection bias because dropouts may differ systematically between groups.
- **C (Exclude only Group 1 nonadherent):** Asymmetric exclusion invalidates the trial by selectively removing participants from only the treatment arm, which would bias the results.
