text: A 37-year-old man comes to the office because of a 3-week history of itchy patches of skin and a burning sensation in his feet. He works as a dishwasher and says he frequently works in wet shoes and socks. Vital signs are within normal limits. Physical examination shows the findings in the photograph; these findings are also present on the soles of both feet. The most appropriate pharmacotherapy for this patient will inhibit the activity of which of the following enzymes?
explanation: Dishwasher with wet socks/shoes, itchy patches, burning feet → tinea pedis (athlete's foot), a dermatophyte fungal infection. Topical terbinafine is first-line — it inhibits squalene monooxygenase (squalene epoxidase), blocking ergosterol synthesis, which is essential for fungal cell membrane integrity. Answer: D (Squalene monooxygenase).
subject: NBME 120

text: A 27-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department because of a 2-week history of double vision. Neurologic examination shows that the left eye does not adduct past the midline on horizontal gaze when the patient looks to the right. Leftward horizontal gaze is normal. This patient's ocular movement deficit is most likely caused by damage to which of the following structures?

options.text: Left nucleus of the abducens nerve
Right nucleus of the abducens nerve

explanation: Left eye does not adduct when looking right (failure of left medial rectus to contract), but leftward gaze is normal (intact left lateral rectus). This pattern = left internuclear ophthalmoplegia (INO). Lesion in left medial longitudinal fasciculus (MLF) disrupts signal from right abducens internuclear neurons to left oculomotor nucleus. Answer: B (Left medial longitudinal fasciculus).
subject: NBME 120

text: A 50-year-old man comes to the office for a follow-up examination. He has a 2-month history of headache and shortness of breath with exertion. He also has hypertension treated with hydrochlorothiazide for the past 2 years. His blood pressure is 180/105 mm Hg. Ophthalmoscopic examination is most likely to show which of the following in this patient?
explanation: Severe hypertension (180/105 mm Hg) with headache and dyspnea → hypertensive retinopathy. Arteriovenous nicking (where the sclerotic arteriole compresses the venule at crossing points) is a classic Grade 2 hypertensive retinopathy finding. Other findings: silver-wiring, flame hemorrhages, cotton-wool spots, papilledema (Grade 4). Answer: A.
subject: NBME 120

text: A 16-day-old male newborn is brought to the office by his parents because of a 2-day history of yellow-tinged skin and dark urine in his diapers. He was delivered via spontaneous vaginal delivery at 36 weeks’ gestation. He weighed 3799 g (8 lb 6 oz; 75th percentile) at birth. He was discharged from the hospital after successfully breast-feeding for 24 hours with normal growth and weight gain. At that time, physical examination showed no abnormalities. Since then, appetite has been normal. Today, he is 51 cm (20 in; 25th percentile) long and weighs 3600 g (7 lb 15 oz; 25th percentile); head circumference is 36 cm (14 in; 75th percentile). Vital signs are within normal limits. Physical examination shows conjunctival icterus. Neurologic examination shows no focal findings. Results of complete blood count are within the reference ranges. Results of serum studies are shown: [[table:0]] 70 U/L (N=10–40) γ-Glutamyltransferase [GGT] 165 U/L (N=13–147) Which of the following is the most likely underlying cause of the findings in this patient?

options.text: Low activity of bile canalicular MRP transporter

explanation: 16-day-old newborn with jaundice, dark urine, conjugated hyperbilirubinemia (direct bilirubin elevated) → obstructive jaundice. Most likely biliary atresia, a surgical emergency requiring Kasai procedure. Extrahepatic bile duct obliteration prevents bile flow → conjugated hyperbilirubinemia, dark urine (bilirubinuria), pale stools. Answer: D (Obstruction of bile flow).
subject: NBME 120

text: A 21-year-old woman comes to the office for an initial examination. Pulse is 80/min, respirations are 14/min, and blood pressure is 220/100 mm Hg. Pulse oximetry on room air shows an oxygen saturation of 99%. Physical examination discloses a faint abdominal bruit. ECG shows left ventricular hypertrophy. Complete blood count and serum concentrations, including electrolytes, urea nitrogen, and creatinine, are within the reference ranges. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's condition?
explanation: Young woman (21), severe hypertension (220/100), abdominal bruit, LVH → renovascular hypertension. In a young woman without atherosclerosis risk factors, fibromuscular dysplasia (FMD) is the most common cause of renal artery stenosis. FMD causes alternating thickening and thinning of arterial wall ('string of beads' on angiography). Answer: B (Fibromuscular dysplasia).
subject: NBME 120

text: In a sample of 100 individuals, the mean leukocyte count is 7500/mm 3, with a standard deviation of 1000/mm 3. If the leukocyte counts in this population follow a normal (gaussian) distribution, approximately 50% of individuals will have which of the following total leukocyte counts?
explanation: In a normal (Gaussian) distribution, the mean = median = mode. Therefore, 50% of values lie below the mean and 50% above. With mean = 7500/mm³, exactly 50% of individuals will have values below 7500/mm³. Answer: D (<7500/mm³).
subject: NBME 120

text: A 10-year-old boy is brought to the physician because of a 3-week history of nosebleeds and easy bruisability. His older brother has had similar episodes. He is at the 30th percentile for height and weight. Physical examination shows nasal and gingival bleeding and several ecchymoses over the trunk and upper and lower extremities in various stages of healing. Laboratory studies show a platelet count of 300,000/mm 3 (N=150,000–400,000). Platelet adhesion testing shows a normal response to ristocetin, but aggregation does not occur in response to thrombin; platelet morphology is normal. Prothrombin time and activated partial thromboplastin time are within the reference ranges. A defect in which of the following is the most likely cause of the findings in this patient?
explanation: Bleeding with normal platelet count, normal ristocetin aggregation (rules out von Willebrand disease), no aggregation to thrombin → Glanzmann thrombasthenia. Autosomal recessive disorder caused by deficiency of glycoprotein IIb-IIIa complex (αIIbβ3 integrin), which is the fibrinogen receptor required for platelet aggregation. Answer: C.
subject: NBME 120

text: A 36-year-old woman of Icelandic descent comes to the physician for genetic counseling after she was diagnosed with invasive ductal carcinoma of the breast. She has no family history of breast cancer. Genetic analysis shows a 999del5 mutation in the BRCA2 gene. This mutation is the cause of 9% of all breast cancers in Iceland. Which of the following best explains the prevalence of this mutation in Iceland?

options.text: A bottleneck reduction in population due to breast cancer occurrences
Genetic heterogeneity of inherited breast/ovarian cancer
Heterozygote advantage due to the mutation
Random mating in a very large population

explanation: A single BRCA2 mutation (999del5) accounts for 9% of all breast cancers in Iceland. This is a classic founder effect: a small, geographically isolated population with limited gene flow leads to a mutation present in a common ancestor being passed to many descendants. Iceland's geographic isolation and small founding population explain this. Answer: C.
subject: NBME 120

text: A previously healthy 65-year-old woman comes to the physician because of several episodes of fainting during the past 2 months. Each episode lasted several minutes. Her pulse is 82/min, respirations are 20/min, and blood pressure is 135/87 mm Hg. Cardiac examination shows S3 and S4. Echocardiography shows a pedunculated intracardiac mass. The lesion is resected. A photomicrograph of the resected lesion is shown. This lesion was most likely obtained from which of the following locations?
explanation: Pedunculated intracardiac mass causing syncope, S3 and S4 gallop → atrial myxoma. Cardiac myxomas are the most common primary cardiac tumor. Approximately 75% occur in the left atrium, typically attached to the interatrial septum near the fossa ovalis. They can prolapse through the mitral valve causing obstruction (syncope). Answer: B (Left atrium).
subject: NBME 120

text: A 45-year-old woman with end-stage renal disease as a result of IgA glomerulopathy is about to receive a kidney transplant. She has been undergoing hemodialysis for 2 years. She also has hypertension well controlled with an ACE inhibitor. Her temperature is 37.5°C (99.5°F), pulse is 88/min, respirations are 14/min, and blood pressure is 138/78 mm Hg. During the operation, the renal vessels are anastomosed, and blood is released into the transplanted kidney. Within 10 minutes, this organ becomes swollen and shows multiple areas of hemorrhage. Which of the following is the most likely cause of these findings in the transplanted kidney?

options.text: Sensitized CD8+ T lymphocytes in the donor
Sensitized CD8+ T lymphocytes in the recipient

explanation: Kidney transplant becomes swollen and hemorrhagic within 10 minutes of reperfusion → hyperacute rejection. Caused by preformed anti-HLA antibodies in the recipient (from prior transfusions, pregnancy, or prior transplantation) that bind to donor endothelial antigens → immediate complement activation, endothelial injury, thrombosis. Answer: D (Preformed antibodies in the recipient).
subject: NBME 120

text: A 65-year-old man comes to the emergency department 30 minutes after the sudden onset of severe pain in his right thigh. He recalls no trauma to the area. He has a 2-year history of multiple myeloma. He is treated with a bisphosphonate medication. Examination of the right thigh shows tenderness and displacement of the femur. X-ray of the right lower extremity shows a midshaft femoral fracture. The most likely cause of this patient's injury is an underlying abnormality of which of the following?
explanation: Multiple myeloma patient on bisphosphonate (likely zoledronic acid or pamidronate) with atraumatic femoral midshaft fracture → atypical femoral fracture. Bisphosphonates suppress osteoclast-mediated bone remodeling, which can lead to overly suppressed bone turnover, accumulation of microdamage, and impaired healing, predisposing to atypical fractures. Answer: A (Bone remodeling).
subject: NBME 120

text: A 45-year-old man comes to the emergency department because of a 4-hour history of left ankle pain and swelling. He recalls twisting his left foot after tripping over one of his children's toys as he walked to the bathroom last night. He cannot bear weight on the left ankle because of pain. Examination of the left ankle shows edema with decreased range of motion in all directions. There is tenderness to palpation just distal to the lateral malleolus. Which of the following is the most likely mechanism of this injury?
explanation: Twisting ankle injury, tenderness distal to lateral malleolus → lateral ankle sprain. The most common mechanism is inversion (supination) stress, which injures the anterior talofibular ligament (ATFL), the weakest lateral ankle ligament. Inversion plantarflexion also risks calcaneofibular ligament injury. Answer: C (Inversion).
subject: NBME 120

text: A previously healthy 3-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department by his parents 30 minutes after the sudden onset of severe coughing and gagging; he had been eating candy. He has vomited once since then. On arrival, he is alert and mildly anxious. He is at the 50th percentile for height and 75th percentile for weight. His temperature is 36.9°C (98.4°F), pulse is 136/min, respirations are 38/min, and blood pressure is 90/48 mm Hg. Pulse oximetry on room air shows an oxygen saturation of 93%. Breath sounds are decreased on the left. The remainder of the examination shows no abnormalities. An x-ray of the chest is shown. Which of the following is the most likely explanation for this patient's oxygen saturation?
explanation: 3-year-old with acute choking on candy, decreased left breath sounds, hypoxia → foreign body aspiration (likely into left main bronchus). Obstruction causes left lung atelectasis and hypoxic vasoconstriction but continued perfusion to non-ventilated alveoli → ventilation-perfusion (V/Q) mismatch → hypoxemia. This is an intrapulmonary right-to-left shunt physiology. Answer: E (Ventilation-perfusion mismatch).
subject: NBME 120

text: A 67-year-old woman with congenital bicuspid aortic valve is admitted to the hospital because of a 2-day history of fever and chills. Current medication is lisinopril. Temperature is 38.0°C (100.4°F), pulse is 90/min, respirations are 20/min, and blood pressure is 110/70 mm Hg. Cardiac examination shows a grade 3/6 systolic murmur that is best heard over the second right intercostal space. Blood culture grows viridans streptococci susceptible to penicillin. In addition to penicillin, an antibiotic synergistic to penicillin is administered that may help shorten the duration of this patient's drug treatment. Which of the following is the most likely mechanism of action of this additional antibiotic on bacteria?
explanation:
This patient with viridans streptococcal endocarditis on a congenital bicuspid valve is being given penicillin plus a synergistic agent. The classic synergistic partner is an aminoglycoside (e.g., gentamicin), which binds the 30S ribosomal subunit and irreversibly inhibits bacterial protein synthesis. Penicillin disrupts the cell wall, which enhances aminoglycoside uptake into the organism, producing bactericidal synergy that can shorten the treatment course.

**(A)** Binding to DNA-dependent RNA polymerase describes rifampin.
**(C)** Competition with p-aminobenzoic acid describes sulfonamides, and **(D)** inhibition of dihydrofolate reductase describes trimethoprim—neither is used for synergy here.
**(E)** Inhibition of DNA gyrase describes fluoroquinolones.
subject: Cardiovascular

text: A 12-year-old girl is brought to the physician because of a 2-month history of intermittent yellowing of the eyes and skin. Physical examination shows no abnormalities except for jaundice. Her serum total bilirubin concentration is 3 mg/dL, with a direct component of 1 mg/dL. Serum studies show a haptoglobin concentration and AST and ALT activities that are within the reference ranges. There is no evidence of injury or exposure to toxins. Which of the following additional findings is most likely in this patient?
explanation:
This adolescent has intermittent, mild, predominantly unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia (total bilirubin 3 mg/dL with direct 1 mg/dL) with a normal haptoglobin and normal AST/ALT. This is classic for Gilbert syndrome, caused by reduced activity of UDP-glucuronosyltransferase (UGT1A1), which impairs bilirubin conjugation and produces episodic jaundice during stress, fasting, or illness.

- **(C) Increased hemolysis** is excluded by the normal haptoglobin.
- **(B) Gallstones** and **(D) Increased serum alkaline phosphatase activity** would point to biliary obstruction with conjugated (direct) hyperbilirubinemia, which is not present.
- **(E) Ineffective erythropoiesis** would also raise indirect bilirubin but typically alters the CBC and haptoglobin and does not fit this otherwise healthy child.
subject: GI

text: During an experiment, drug X is added to a muscle bath containing a strip of guinea pig intestinal smooth muscle. Agonists are added to the bath, and the resultant effects on muscle tension are shown in the table. [[table:0]] Which of the following types of drugs is most likely to produce effects most similar to those of drug X?
explanation: In the muscle bath, drug X markedly augments the contractile response to acetylcholine (tension rose from 11.3 to 18.5 g) while leaving the responses to vehicle and norepinephrine essentially unchanged. Selectively potentiating the cholinergic response indicates that drug X prevents acetylcholine breakdown—the action of a cholinesterase inhibitor, which increases synaptic acetylcholine. (E) A muscarinic antagonist would blunt, not amplify, the acetylcholine response. (A) α1- and (B) β-adrenergic antagonists act on the adrenergic limb (norepinephrine), which was unaffected. (D) A monoamine oxidase inhibitor raises catecholamine levels and would not selectively enhance acetylcholine.
subject: General Principles

text: A 30-year-old woman, gravida 2, para 0, aborta 1, at 28 weeks' gestation comes to the office for a prenatal visit. She has had one previous pregnancy resulting in a spontaneous abortion at 12 weeks' gestation. Today, her vital signs are within normal limits. Physical examination shows a uterus consistent in size with a 28-week gestation. Fetal ultrasonography shows a male fetus with no abnormalities. Her blood group is O, Rh-negative. The father's blood group is B, Rh-positive. The physician recommends administration of Rho(D) immune globulin to the patient. This treatment is most likely to prevent which of the following in this mother?

options.text: Generation of IgM antibodies from fixing complement in the fetus
Immunosuppression caused by RhD on erythrocytes from the fetus

explanation:
This Rh-negative mother is carrying an Rh-positive fetus. Rho(D) immune globulin (anti-D) is a preparation of human IgG antibodies against the D antigen. When administered to the mother, it binds any fetal RhD-positive erythrocytes that enter the maternal circulation (e.g., during delivery, trauma, or procedures) and facilitates their clearance by the reticuloendothelial system before the maternal immune system can mount a primary response. This prevents the mother from forming memory B cells and anti-RhD IgG antibodies, thereby protecting future Rh-positive pregnancies from hemolytic disease of the newborn (erythroblastosis fetalis).

Distractors:
A. Development of natural killer cells — Anti-D does not target or suppress NK cell development; NK cells are part of innate immunity and are not the effectors of Rh sensitization.
B. Development of polycythemia — Polycythemia is not a consequence of Rh sensitization; hemolytic disease of the newborn causes anemia and hyperbilirubinemia, not polycythemia.
D. Generation of IgM antibodies from fixing complement in the fetus — The pathophysiologic concern is maternal anti-D IgG (not IgM) crossing the placenta and causing fetal hemolysis; anti-D prevents maternal sensitization, not complement fixation by fetal antibodies.
E. Immunosuppression caused by RhD on erythrocytes from the fetus — RhD is a red cell surface antigen, not an immunosuppressive molecule; anti-D does not prevent immunosuppression.
subject: Reproductive/Endocrine

text: A 55-year-old man is brought to the emergency department because of shortness of breath and confusion for 4 hours. He has hypertension and chronic kidney disease requiring hemodialysis. An ECG shows low voltage with electrical alternans. Physical examination is most likely to show which of the following findings?
explanation:
Low-voltage QRS complexes with electrical alternans on ECG in a dialysis patient strongly suggest a large pericardial effusion with cardiac tamponade (uremic pericarditis). Cardiac tamponade impairs diastolic filling, producing hypotension (85/60 mm Hg), reflex tachycardia (120/min), elevated jugular venous pressure from impaired right heart filling, and an exaggerated (increased) pulsus paradoxus from enhanced ventricular interdependence. These findings match option A.

**Distractors:** Options B and C are incorrect because tamponade classically produces an increased pulsus paradoxus, not a normal one. Options C, E, and F are incorrect because JVP is elevated in tamponade. Options D, E, and F are incorrect because normal blood pressure and heart rate are inconsistent with the hemodynamic compromise of tamponade, which characteristically causes hypotension and reflex tachycardia.
subject: Cardiovascular

text: A 52-year-old woman begins pharmacotherapy after being diagnosed with type 2 diabetes mellitus. Four weeks later, her hepatic glucose output is decreased, and target tissue glucose uptake and utilization are increased. Which of the following drugs was most likely prescribed for this patient?
explanation: After 4 weeks of therapy this patient has decreased hepatic glucose output and increased peripheral glucose uptake and utilization—the hallmark actions of metformin, a biguanide that reduces hepatic gluconeogenesis and improves insulin sensitivity in muscle and adipose tissue. (B) Glyburide, (D) nateglinide, and (E) repaglinide are insulin secretagogues that act on pancreatic beta cells rather than primarily reducing hepatic output. (A) Acarbose works in the gut lumen by inhibiting α-glucosidase to slow carbohydrate absorption.
subject: Reproductive/Endocrine
concept_fingerprint: metformin mechanism hepatic gluconeogenesis peripheral uptake

text: An asymptomatic 44-year-old man is found to have HIV infection during routine screening prior to donating blood. A complete blood count done at the time of the screening shows: [[table:0]] Which of the following physical findings is most likely in this patient?
explanation: This patient has isolated severe thrombocytopenia (platelets 15,000/mm³) with a normal prothrombin and partial thromboplastin time, a picture consistent with HIV-associated immune thrombocytopenia. A platelet (primary hemostasis) defect produces mucocutaneous bleeding, most characteristically petechiae. (B) Hemarthrosis and (E) visceral hematoma reflect coagulation factor (secondary hemostasis) defects, which would prolong the PT or PTT—both normal here. (A) Deep venous thrombosis is a thrombotic, not bleeding, complication, and (D) subungual (splinter) hemorrhage is associated with endocarditis or trauma rather than thrombocytopenia.
subject: Hemat/Lymph/Immune

text: A 23-year-old woman with bone marrow failure is treated with a large dose of rabbit antithymocyte globulin. Ten days later, she develops fever, lymphadenopathy, arthralgias, and erythema on her hands and feet. Which of the following is the most likely cause of these symptoms?

options.text: Cytokine secretion by natural killer cells

explanation: Ten days after receiving rabbit antithymocyte globulin (a foreign serum protein), this patient developed fever, lymphadenopathy, arthralgias, and an acral rash—classic serum sickness. Serum sickness is a type III hypersensitivity reaction in which antigen–antibody (immune) complexes deposit in tissues and activate complement, producing the delayed multisystem inflammation. (A) NK cytokine secretion and (D) polyclonal T-cell activation describe cytokine release reactions that occur much sooner. (B) Eosinophil degranulation underlies type I allergic reactions, and (E) widespread B-cell apoptosis does not explain this immune-complex syndrome.
subject: Multisystem

text: After being severely beaten and sustaining a gunshot wound to the abdomen, a 42-year-old woman undergoes resection of a perforated small bowel. During the operation, plastic reconstruction of facial fractures, and open reduction and internal fixation of the left femur are also done. Thirty-six hours postoperatively, she is awake but not completely alert. She is receiving intravenous morphine via a patient-controlled pump. She says that she needs the morphine to treat her pain, but she is worried that she is becoming addicted. She has no history of substance use disorder. She drinks one to two glasses of wine weekly. Which of the following initial actions by the physician is most appropriate?

options.text: Reassure the patient that her chance of becoming addicted to narcotics is minuscule
Maintain the morphine, but periodically administer intravenous naloxone
Switch the patient to oral acetaminophen as soon as she can take medication orally
Switch the patient to intramuscular lorazepam
Switch the patient to intravenous phenobarbital

explanation: This patient is experiencing severe acute postoperative pain, has no history of a substance use disorder, and is appropriately using patient-controlled morphine. The risk of developing addiction (a behavioral disorder) from short-term opioids used to treat genuine acute pain is extremely low, so the most appropriate first action is to reassure her and continue effective analgesia. (B) Periodic naloxone would precipitate withdrawal and uncontrolled pain. (C) Switching prematurely to acetaminophen would undertreat severe pain. (D) Lorazepam and (E) phenobarbital are sedatives that do not treat pain and add respiratory depression risk.
subject: General Principles

text: A 22-year-old woman comes to the office because of a 4-day history of an itchy, red rash on her right arm. She has no history of major medical illness and takes no medications. She says she has recently used a new hair dye. She is 165 cm (5 ft 5 in) tall and weighs 61 kg (135 lb); BMI is 23 kg/m2. Her temperature is 37.0°C (98.6°F), pulse is 70/min. respirations are 22/min, and blood pressure is 115/70 mm Hg. Examination of the right forearm shows the findings in the photograph. Which of the following ligand → receptor pairs most likely played a primary role in the proliferation of the T lymphocytes present at the site of the rash in this patient?

options.text: CD2 on T lymphocytes → intercellular adhesion molecule (ICAM)-3 on epidermal Langerhans cells
CD28 on T lymphocytes → CD80 on epidermal Langerhans cells
CD40L on T lymphocytes → CD40 on epidermal Langerhans cells
CD45 on T lymphocytes → CD28 on epidermal Langerhans cells
Lymphocyte function-associated antigen-1 on T lymphocytes → ICAM1 on epidermal Langerhans cells

explanation:
This patient has allergic contact dermatitis to hair dye, a type IV (delayed) hypersensitivity reaction in which T lymphocytes proliferate at the site of antigen exposure. Full T-cell activation and proliferation require two signals: antigen-specific signal 1 (T-cell receptor–MHC interaction) and a costimulatory signal 2. The primary costimulatory signal is provided by **CD28 on the T lymphocyte engaging CD80 (B7-1) on the antigen-presenting epidermal Langerhans cell**. Therefore, **option B is correct**.

**(A) CD2–ICAM-3** and **(E) LFA-1–ICAM-1** mediate adhesion between T cells and antigen-presenting cells but do not deliver the key costimulatory signal required for T-cell proliferation. **(C) CD40L–CD40** signaling primarily activates B cells and macrophages and supports helper T-cell function but is not the primary proliferation signal for T cells. **(D) CD45–CD28** is not a physiologic ligand–receptor pair.
subject: Hemat/Lymph/Immune

text: Six healthy subjects participate in a study of muscle metabolism during which hyperglycemia and hyperinsulinemia is induced. Muscle biopsy specimens obtained from the subjects during the resting state show significantly increased concentrations of malonyl-CoA. The increased malonyl-CoA concentration most likely directly inhibits which of the following processes in these subjects?
explanation:
Under hyperglycemic, hyperinsulinemic (fed) conditions, malonyl-CoA concentrations rise. Malonyl-CoA directly inhibits **carnitine palmitoyltransferase I (CPT I)**, the enzyme that transports long-chain fatty acids into mitochondria, thereby blocking **fatty acid oxidation**. This coordinates metabolism so that in the fed state the body synthesizes rather than burns fatty acids.

**(B) Fatty acid synthesis** is promoted, not inhibited, because malonyl-CoA is the committed substrate for that pathway. Malonyl-CoA does not directly inhibit **(C) gluconeogenesis**, **(D) glycogenolysis**, **(E) glycolysis**, or **(F) oxidative phosphorylation**.
subject: General Principles
concept_fingerprint: malonyl-CoA CPTI fatty acid oxidation inhibition fed state

text: Over 1 year, a study is conducted to assess the antileukemic activity of a new tyrosine kinase inhibitor in patients with chronic myeloid leukemia in blast crisis. All patients enrolled in the study are informed that they would be treated with the tyrosine kinase inhibitor. They are assigned to successive dose cohorts of 300 to 1000 mg/day of the drug. Six to eight patients are assigned to each dose. Treatment efficacy is determined based on the results of complete blood counts and bone marrow assessments conducted regularly throughout the study. This study is best described as which of the following?
explanation: In this study every enrolled patient is told they will receive the tyrosine kinase inhibitor, patients are placed into successive dose-escalation cohorts, and there is no control group and no randomization or blinding. These features define an open-labeled clinical trial (a typical phase I dose-finding design). (A) A case-control study looks backward from outcome to exposure. (D) A randomized clinical trial and (E) a single-blind, randomized, controlled trial both require randomization (and blinding for the latter). (B) A crossover study would have each patient switch between treatments.
subject: General Principles
concept_fingerprint: phase I open label dose escalation trial

text: A 63-year-old man is brought to the emergency department because of a 4-day history of increasingly severe left leg pain and swelling of his left calf. He also has a 1-month history of increasingly severe upper midthoracic back pain. During this time, he has had a 9-kg (20-lb) weight loss despite no change in appetite. He has no history of major medical illness. His only medication is ibuprofen. He is 180 cm (5 ft 11 in) tall and weighs 82 kg (180 lb); BMI is 25 kg/m2. His vital signs are within normal limits. On examination, lower extremity pulses are palpable bilaterally. The remainder of the physical examination shows no abnormalities. An x-ray of the thoracic spine shows no abnormalities. A CT scan of the abdomen shows a 3-cm mass in the body of the pancreas; there are liver metastases and encasement of the superior mesenteric artery. Ultrasonography of the left lower extremity shows a femoropopliteal venous clot. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient’s symptoms?

options.text: Splenic artery aneurysm and embolic disease of the left lower extremity

explanation:
This patient with pancreatic adenocarcinoma and liver metastases developed a lower-extremity deep venous thrombosis—an example of cancer-associated hypercoagulability (Trousseau syndrome). Advanced malignancies, especially pancreatic and other adenocarcinomas, release procoagulant factors (such as tissue factor and mucins) that produce migratory or unprovoked venous thromboses.

**Distractors:**
- **(A) Carcinoid syndrome** causes flushing, diarrhea, and bronchoconstriction, not thrombosis.
- **(C) Multiple endocrine neoplasia** produces endocrine tumors (e.g., medullary thyroid carcinoma, pheochromocytoma, pancreatic neuroendocrine tumors), not this presentation of adenocarcinoma with DVT.
- **(D) Splenic artery aneurysm and embolic disease** would cause arterial, not venous, occlusion and does not explain a femoropopliteal venous clot.
- **(E) Superior mesenteric artery syndrome** (compression of the duodenum between the SMA and aorta) causes obstructive symptoms, not lower-extremity venous thrombosis.
subject: Multisystem

text: A 40-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a 6-month history of increased facial hair growth. Her last menstrual period was 4 months ago. She is 165 cm (5 ft 5 in) tall and weighs 70 kg (154 lb); BMI is 26 kg/m2. Her pulse is 80/min, and blood pressure is 130/82 mm Hg. Physical examination shows temporal balding and coarse dark hair on the upper lip and chin. Pelvic examination shows clitoral enlargement. Her serum testosterone concentration is increased. Serum concentrations of androstenedione, dehydroepiandrosterone, and urinary 17-ketosteroids are within the reference ranges. Ultrasonography of the pelvis shows a 12-cm ovarian mass. Which of the following best describes this mass?
explanation: Rapid virilization (hirsutism, temporal balding, clitoromegaly) with a markedly increased serum testosterone but normal androstenedione, DHEA, and urinary 17-ketosteroids localizes the androgen source to the ovary rather than the adrenal gland. A solid 12-cm ovarian mass producing testosterone is most consistent with a Sertoli-Leydig cell tumor (androblastoma). (A) Granulosa cell tumors and (E) thecomas typically secrete estrogen and cause feminization or bleeding. (D) Teratomas are germ cell tumors with mixed tissue, and (B) ovarian carcinoid secretes serotonin, not testosterone.
subject: Reproductive/Endocrine

text: A 35-year-old man comes to the physician because of pain and swelling of his right arm where he scraped it on a tree branch 2 days ago. His temperature is 38.3°C (101°F). Examination of the right forearm shows edema around a fluctuant erythematous lesion at the site of trauma. The area is extremely tender to palpation. Which of the following is most likely the primary mechanism of the development of edema in this patient?
explanation:
The painful, fluctuant, erythematous, edematous lesion reflects **acute inflammation**. The principal mechanism of inflammatory edema is **increased vascular permeability** produced by histamine-mediated contraction of endothelial cells, which widens (separates) interendothelial junctions in postcapillary venules and allows protein-rich fluid to leak into tissue (an **exudate**).

- **(C) Increased hydrostatic pressure** produces a protein-poor **transudate**, not an inflammatory exudate.
- **(B) Disruption of vascular basement membranes** is not the primary early mechanism of edema in acute inflammation.
- **(A) Degranulation of eosinophils** drives allergic and parasitic responses, not typical bacterial acute inflammation.
- **(D) Release of thromboxane** mainly promotes platelet aggregation and vasoconstriction, not vascular permeability.
subject: General Principles

text: A 12-year-old boy is brought to the physician because of a 2-month history of headaches and a 6-day history of nausea and vomiting. Funduscopic examination shows bilateral papilledema. He walks with a broad-based gait. An MRI of the brain shows a tumor in the pineal region compressing the brain stem and leading to hydrocephalus. This patient most likely has impairment of which of the following oculomotor functions?
explanation:
A pineal-region tumor compresses the dorsal midbrain (tectal plate), producing **Parinaud syndrome**. The hallmark of this syndrome is paralysis of conjugate **upward gaze** due to involvement of the superior colliculus and pretectal area. The mass also obstructs the cerebral aqueduct, causing the hydrocephalus, papilledema, headaches, and vomiting seen here.

**Distractors:**
- **(A) Abduction:** Mediated by cranial nerve VI (abducens), which is not the structure compressed by a pineal mass.
- **(B) Horizontal pursuit:** Depends on frontal eye fields and pontine gaze centers, not the tectal plate.
- **(C) Optokinetic nystagmus:** Involves cortical and subcortical pathways that are not the characteristic deficit of dorsal midbrain compression.
- **(E) Vestibulo-ocular reflex:** Relies on vestibular nuclei and brainstem reflex arcs; while intact brainstem pathways are required, loss of the VOR is not the defining feature of Parinaud syndrome.
subject: Behavioral/Nervous & Special Senses

text: A 52-year-old man comes to the emergency department because of a 1-day history of nausea, vomiting, and right- sided abdominal pain that radiates to his back. He has not had fever or increased urinary frequency. He has a history of type 2 diabetes mellitus, hyperlipidemia, hypertension, and atrial fibrillation. Current medications are atorvastatin, glyburide, hydrochlorothiazide, lisinopril, and warfarin. He smoked 1½ packs of cigarettes daily for 35 years until he quit 6 months ago. He has had no recent alcoholic beverage or illicit drug use. He is 188 cm (6 ft 2 in) tall and weighs 109 kg (240 lb); BMI is 31 kg/m2. Temperature is 36.4°C (97.6°F), pulse is 88/min, respirations are 20/min, and blood pressure is 165/92 mm Hg. Pulse oximetry on room air shows an oxygen saturation of 96%. Physical examination discloses right upper quadrant and flank tenderness but no rebound tenderness or guarding. CT scan of the abdomen with and without contrast shows an enlarged right kidney and wedge-shaped areas of hypodensity; there is no evidence of nephrolithiasis. Which of the following is the strongest predisposing risk factor for this patient's condition?
explanation: The CT shows an enlarged kidney with wedge-shaped areas of hypodensity and no stones—findings of renal infarction from thromboembolism. Among this patient's conditions, atrial fibrillation is the strongest predisposing risk factor because it promotes intracardiac thrombus formation that can embolize to the renal artery. (B) Hyperlipidemia, (C) hypertension, (D) past smoking, and (E) type 2 diabetes contribute to chronic atherosclerotic disease but are far weaker direct causes of an acute embolic renal infarct than atrial fibrillation.
subject: Renal/Urinary

text: A 24-year-old man comes to the office because of a 2-day history of a red, itchy rash on his buttocks and legs. Four days ago, he returned from a cruise to the Caribbean, during which he swam in the ship’s pool and used the hot tub. He appears well. His vital signs are within normal limits. Physical examination shows the findings in the photograph. The infectious agent causing these findings most likely began to proliferate in which of the following locations?
explanation:
This pruritic rash after hot tub and pool exposure is classic for **hot tub folliculitis** caused by *Pseudomonas aeruginosa*. The organism proliferates in inadequately chlorinated warm water and infects the **hair follicles**, producing follicular papules and pustules in the distribution of submerged skin.

**Distractors:**
- **A. Apocrine gland** — Found mainly in axillae and anogenital regions; not the primary site for this diffuse truncal and leg rash.
- **B. Dermis** — Dermal infections (e.g., cellulitis) present as spreading erythema and edema, not discrete follicular papulopustules.
- **C. Eccrine gland** — Sweat ducts are affected in miliaria (heat rash), which is noninfectious and caused by duct obstruction, not by Pseudomonas proliferation.
- **E. Sebaceous gland** — Associated with acne vulgaris and sebaceous hyperplasia; *P. aeruginosa* hot tub folliculitis specifically targets the hair follicle rather than the sebaceous unit.
subject: MSK/Skin
concept_fingerprint: Pseudomonas hot tub folliculitis hair follicle

text: An otherwise healthy 45-year-old man comes to the physician because of a 3-week history of progressive epigastric heartburn and a 4.5-kg (10-lb) weight loss. The pain tends to be more severe at night and occurs 1 to 3 hours after meals during the day. He has had similar episodes with lesser intensity during the past year. Abdominal examination shows tenderness to deep palpation. Test of the stool for occult blood is positive. Endoscopy shows a bleeding 3-cm ulcer in the antrum of the stomach. A photomicrograph of Steiner silver-stained tissue (400x) from a biopsy of the gastric mucosa adjacent to the ulcer is shown. Which of the following processes is most likely to be involved?

options.text: Elaboration of proteases and urease with local tissue destruction
Ingestion of preformed toxins in contaminated well water

explanation: A bleeding antral gastric ulcer with Steiner silver-stained organisms indicates *Helicobacter pylori* infection. *H. pylori* produces urease (which neutralizes gastric acid and supports colonization) along with proteases and other enzymes that, together with the host inflammatory response, cause local mucosal tissue destruction and ulceration. (B) Hyperacidity alone does not explain the silver-stained organisms, (C) preformed toxins describe other foodborne illnesses, and (D) spirochete invasion of gastric cells describes a different organism—*H. pylori* is a curved gram-negative bacillus that is largely noninvasive.
subject: GI

text: A 14-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department after being hit with a baseball bat on the lateral side of his leg immediately below the knee. He is unable to dorsiflex his foot. Which of the following nerves is most likely injured?
explanation: A blow to the lateral leg just below the knee strikes the common fibular (peroneal) nerve as it wraps around the neck of the fibula, where it is superficial and vulnerable. Injury impairs the muscles of the anterior and lateral compartments, producing foot drop with inability to dorsiflex (and evert) the foot. (B) The femoral and (C) obturator nerves act at the thigh, (D) the sural nerve is purely sensory, and (E) the tibial nerve controls plantar flexion rather than dorsiflexion.
subject: MSK/Skin

text: A 26-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department because of an 8-hour history of severe back and abdominal pain and mild but persistent vaginal bleeding. Ultrasonography of the abdomen shows a 2-cm ectopic pregnancy in the ampulla. The ampulla has ruptured into the surrounding tissue. Fluid from this rupture will most likely be found in which of the following locations?
explanation: A ruptured ampullary ectopic pregnancy spills blood into the peritoneal cavity, where it collects in the most dependent recess. In a woman this is the rectouterine pouch (of Douglas), located between the rectum and the uterus, so culdocentesis or imaging finds fluid there. (A) The lesser peritoneal cavity (omental bursa) is in the upper abdomen and does not communicate directly with this pelvic bleeding. (B) The mesometrium is part of the broad ligament, not a dependent fluid collection site. (D) The uterine cavity and (E) the vagina are part of the reproductive tract lumen, not the peritoneal space into which the tube ruptured.
subject: Reproductive/Endocrine

text: A 46-year-old woman with active ankylosing spondylitis comes to the office for a follow-up examination. The use of various conventional nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs has been ineffective. Sulfasalazine treatment also has not resulted in improvement. The most appropriate next step in treatment is administration of a drug that inhibits which of the following?
explanation:
This patient has active ankylosing spondylitis that has failed both NSAIDs and sulfasalazine. The next step is a biologic agent that inhibits tumor necrosis factor α (e.g., infliximab, etanercept, adalimumab), which is highly effective in axial spondyloarthritis.

**Distractors:**
- **(B) Cyclooxygenase-2** inhibition is just another NSAID and has already failed.
- **(A) CD20** inhibition (rituximab) is used in rheumatoid arthritis and certain other conditions, not first-line for AS.
- **(E) IL-1** inhibition is used for gout and autoinflammatory syndromes.
- **(C) CTLA-4** (abatacept) and **(D) EGF** inhibition are not standard treatments for ankylosing spondylitis.
subject: MSK/Skin

text: A 55-year-old man comes to the physician because of a 2-week history of recurrent, widespread blister formation. Physical examination shows lesions that are most numerous in the flexural areas including the axillae and groin. The blisters do not break easily, and there are no oral lesions. These blisters are most likely the result of adhesion failure involving which of the following?
explanation:
Tense bullae that do not rupture easily, a flexural distribution, and the absence of oral lesions in an older adult are characteristic of **bullous pemphigoid**. The blisters form because autoantibodies target hemidesmosomal proteins (BP180/BP230) at the **basement membrane** zone, causing subepidermal separation.

**Distractors:**
- **B. Dermal papillae**, **C. Langerhans cells**, **D. Melanocytes**, and **E. Merkel cells** are not the adhesion structures involved in this disease process.

By contrast, pemphigus vulgaris targets intraepidermal desmosomes, producing fragile bullae with frequent oral involvement.
subject: MSK/Skin

text: A 17-year-old girl is brought to the emergency department 30 minutes after her boyfriend found her unconscious next to an empty bottle of acetaminophen. It is suspected that she ingested the tablets approximately 12 hours ago. Her serum acetaminophen concentration is markedly increased. Treatment with activated charcoal and acetylcysteine is initiated. Approximately 48 hours later, the patient develops jaundice, and her serum AST activity is 3000 U/L. Which of the following best explains the jaundice in this patient?
explanation: This patient has fulminant acetaminophen-induced hepatocellular injury, reflected by the AST of 3000 U/L. Severely damaged hepatocytes lose their capacity to take up and conjugate bilirubin, so unconjugated (and some conjugated) bilirubin accumulates and produces jaundice—best described as decreased bilirubin conjugation by failing hepatocytes. Increased hemolysis (D) is not indicated. Activation of biliverdin reductase (A) and decreased urobilinogen generation (C) do not explain the jaundice. The toxicity actually depletes, rather than increases, hepatic glutathione (E).
subject: GI

text: A 72-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a 3-day history of fever, shortness of breath, difficulty swallowing, chest pain, and cough. She is frail. Physical examination shows tachypnea and equal pulses bilaterally. Percussion of the chest shows dullness over the right lower lung field. Laboratory studies show arterial hypoxemia and decreased PCO2. A chest x-ray shows an area of opacification in the lower region of the right lung. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's condition?
explanation: A frail elderly woman with dysphagia and a right lower lobe infiltrate most likely has aspiration pneumonia. Aspirated material preferentially enters the right lower lobe because the right mainstem bronchus is wider, shorter, and more vertical, and impaired swallowing increases aspiration risk. (C) Cigarette smoking and (D) emphysema cause chronic obstructive changes rather than a focal acute infiltrate. (A) Alveolar proteinosis and (E) vasculitis are uncommon and do not fit this acute, focal, dependent-lobe presentation with dysphagia.
subject: Respiratory

text: A 62-year-old man is admitted to the hospital for evaluation of abdominal pain. During the interview, he responds to the questions with a single word and sometimes with sarcastic answers. He does not engage in eye contact, and he frowns as he tells the physician that this is the third time he has been asked these questions. Which of the following is the most appropriate response by the physician?

options.text: "Can you tell me more about your abdominal pain?"
"I understand that you do not feel well, but I need to get a history here."
"I'll come back once you've calmed down, and we can talk more then."
"Listen, if you choose not to cooperate, I'm not going to be able to help you."
"You sound upset. Tell me a little more about that."

explanation: The patient is displaying irritation and frustration. The most therapeutic response names and explores the emotion—'You sound upset. Tell me a little more about that'—which validates his feelings and builds rapport so the interview can proceed. The other replies are nonempathic: (A) ignores his emotion, (B) and (C) are dismissive or postpone care, and (D) is confrontational and threatens to withhold help. Acknowledging and exploring affect is the preferred communication technique.
subject: Behavioral/Nervous & Special Senses

text: A 54-year-old man comes to the physician because of episodes of fainting for 3 months. He also has had difficulty performing daily tasks because he is easily fatigued. He had a myocardial infarction 12 years ago. His pulse is 40/min, respirations are 18/min, and blood pressure is 138/85 mm Hg. Physical examination shows evidence of cannon a waves. An ECG shows a P-wave rate of 90/min, and an R-wave rate of 40/min, with no apparent relation between the two. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Syncope and fatigue with a pulse of 40/min, cannon a waves, and an ECG showing atrial (P) and ventricular (R) rates that are independent of one another (90 vs 40 with no relationship) indicate complete atrioventricular dissociation—third-degree (complete) AV block. (A) First-degree block only prolongs the PR interval. (C) Type I and (D) type II second-degree blocks show some conducted beats with a relationship between P waves and QRS complexes. (B) Right bundle branch block does not cause AV dissociation or this profound bradycardia.
subject: Cardiovascular

text: A 42-year-old woman comes to the physician for a routine examination. She says that she has felt well except for occasional episodes of constipation, abdominal discomfort, and mild fatigue. She was treated for a renal calculus 10 years ago and was told she had a "lazy gallbladder." Her pulse is 82/min, and blood pressure is 150/80 mm Hg. Physical examination shows no other abnormalities. Laboratory studies show: [[table:0]] The most likely cause of this patient's condition is a small, well-defined nodule in which of the following locations?
explanation:
Hypercalcemia (calcium 12 mg/dL) with hypophosphatemia, a history of nephrolithiasis, constipation, and fatigue is the classic "stones, bones, abdominal groans" picture of primary hyperparathyroidism. The cause is most often a small, well-defined parathyroid adenoma that autonomously secretes parathyroid hormone, raising calcium and lowering phosphate.

Distractors: An adrenal nodule (A) would cause catecholamine or cortisol excess, not primary hyperparathyroidism. An anterior pituitary nodule (B) would cause pituitary hormone excess or deficiency. Gallbladder pathology (C) may cause biliary symptoms but does not produce hypercalcemia. A renal lesion (D) does not autonomously secrete PTH and would not produce this specific calcium–phosphate profile as the underlying cause of chronic primary hyperparathyroidism. A thymic nodule (F) is associated with myasthenia gravis or paraneoplastic syndromes, not autonomous PTH secretion.
subject: Reproductive/Endocrine

text: A 72-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department by her husband because of a 1-hour history of difficulty walking and speaking. The husband says that she was well last night but when she awoke this morning, she had difficulty getting out of bed and her speech was slurred. She has a 20-year history of type 2 diabetes mellitus well controlled with medication and diet. She is alert and oriented and is able to follow commands and respond verbally, but she has impaired speech. Her pulse is 80/min, respirations are 16/min, and blood pressure is 142/88 mm Hg. Physical examination shows left-sided hemiparesis. The tongue deviates to the right when protruded. Sensation to pinprick and temperature is normal, and proprioception and sensation to light touch are absent over the left upper and lower extremities. Which of the following labeled sites in the photograph of a cross section of a normal brain stem is most likely damaged in this patient?
explanation:
This patient has contralateral (left) hemiparesis, loss of contralateral proprioception and light touch with preserved pain and temperature, and a tongue that deviates toward the lesioned (right) side—medial medullary syndrome from anterior spinal artery territory infarction. The damaged structures (pyramid/corticospinal tract, medial lemniscus, and hypoglossal fibers) lie in the medial medulla, corresponding to labeled site C. The lateral medullary structures, which would produce a different crossed sensory pattern with pain/temperature loss, are not affected here.

Distractors: Site A likely corresponds to an anterior or anteromedial structure such as the pyramid; damage isolated to this area would cause contralateral hemiparesis but cannot explain the contralateral loss of proprioception/light touch or the ipsilateral tongue deviation. Site B likely points to a more restricted medial or periventricular structure; involvement limited to this site would not simultaneously affect the corticospinal tract, medial lemniscus, and hypoglossal fibers. Site D likely lies in the lateral medulla (e.g., inferior olivary or adjacent region); damage there would produce lateral medullary (Wallenberg) syndrome with vertigo, dysphagia, ipsilateral facial pain/temperature loss, and contralateral body pain/temperature loss—findings absent in this patient. Site E likely corresponds to a lateral sensory tract such as the spinothalamic tract or spinal trigeminal nucleus/tract; damage here would impair pain and temperature sensation rather than proprioception and light touch, and would not cause hemiparesis or tongue deviation.
subject: Behavioral/Nervous & Special Senses

text: A 68-year-old woman with end-stage renal disease comes to the office for a follow-up examination. She has required hemodialysis for the past year. Initially, she did well, but within the past 3 months, she has been admitted to the hospital for fluid overload because of poor adherence to fluid and salt restrictions. She says, "I'm so sick of being on dialysis. Following the restrictions is really hard." Which of the following is the most appropriate initial response by the physician?

options.text: "I imagine being on dialysis is frustrating, but you don't want to die from kidney disease, do you?"
"I know that this is challenging, but do you remember how difficult it is to be hospitalized?"
"It is tough to change your diet and fluid intake, but what sorts of things were you doing at first when you were following the recommendations?"
"Making these changes is so difficult. Can you imagine how good you will feel once you make the changes again?"
"This is very hard to do, but you may have an easier time if you met with the dietician again."

explanation:
This dialysis patient is voicing frustration and nonadherence. The best initial response is empathic and patient-centered, using motivational interviewing to explore what previously helped her succeed. Option C builds on her own prior success and engages her in problem-solving without being confrontational.

**Distractors:** Option A induces guilt and fear by implying she will die. Option B uses fear of hospitalization and is not patient-centered. Option D is leading and prescriptive. Option E jumps to a referral before understanding her perspective and barriers.
subject: General Principles

text: During an experiment, a Southern blot analysis is done by digesting DNA samples with a single restriction endonuclease, separating the digestion products by gel electrophoresis, and transferring them to a filter. The investigator probes the filter by exposing it to a cDNA clone that encodes a single immunoglobulin-constant region. The figure shows the resulting pattern with DNA samples isolated from different organs. Assuming there were no technical errors, the Southern blot analysis results demonstrate which of the following processes?
explanation: On the Southern blot, DNA from different tissues probed for a single immunoglobulin constant region yields different band patterns—lymphoid DNA differs from the germline configuration seen in other organs. This demonstrates somatic V(D)J gene rearrangement, which physically rearranges immunoglobulin gene segments in developing B lymphocytes and alters restriction fragment sizes. (A) Affinity maturation and (E) somatic hypermutation involve point mutations, not large rearrangements detectable this way; (B) apoptosis and (D) RNA splicing do not change genomic DNA restriction patterns.
subject: Hemat/Lymph/Immune

text: A 17-year-old girl has never had a menstrual period. Physical examination shows a normal female body habitus, normal breast development, and normal appearing external genitalia. She has no axillary or pubic hair. The patient refuses to have a pelvic or rectal examination. Which of the following is the most likely explanation for the clinical presentation?
explanation:
A phenotypic female with primary amenorrhea, normal breast development, normal external female genitalia, and absent axillary and pubic hair is the classic picture of complete androgen insensitivity syndrome. These 46,XY individuals have testes that produce testosterone, but a defective androgen receptor prevents virilization and sexual hair development, while peripheral aromatization of androgens to estrogen supports breast development.

**Distractors:**
- **(B) Congenital adrenal hyperplasia:** causes virilization (e.g., clitoromegaly, hirsutism), which is inconsistent with normal female external genitalia and absent sexual hair.
- **(C) Ectodermal dysplasia:** affects ectodermal structures but does not produce this endocrine pattern of normal estrogenization with primary amenorrhea and absent androgenic hair.
- **(D) A psychiatric disorder:** would not account for the consistent physical finding of absent pubic and axillary hair alongside normal breast development.
- **(E) A sex chromosome mosaicism:** does not explain this specific, classic combination of intact estrogenic effects with absent androgenic effects.
subject: Reproductive/Endocrine

text: A 16-year-old boy is brought to the physician because of a 3-day history of abdominal pain and vomiting; he also has had decreased appetite during this period. The pain was initially on the right but now has become generalized. His temperature is 38.8°C (101.8°F), pulse is 100/min, respirations are 20/min, and blood pressure is 143/83 mm Hg. Abdominal examination shows guarding with diffuse rebound tenderness. There are no palpable masses. A CT scan of the abdomen shows a perforated appendix. Examination of peritoneal fluid from this patient will most likely show which of the following organisms?
explanation: A perforated appendix releases colonic flora into the peritoneum, producing polymicrobial peritonitis. The organism most likely recovered is **Escherichia coli**, the predominant facultative gram-negative bacillus of the colonic flora (typically alongside anaerobes such as *Bacteroides fragilis*). *Candida albicans*, *Staphylococcus aureus*, and *Streptococcus pneumoniae* are not typical enteric perforation pathogens. *Citrobacter freundii* is a far less common isolate than *E. coli*.
subject: GI
concept_fingerprint: secondary peritonitis colonic flora E coli

text: A 45-year-old woman comes to the office because of a 6-month history of hot flashes, night sweats, and insomnia. She has not had a menstrual period during this time. She thinks she is going through menopause and asks the physician if there are any medications that will alleviate her symptoms. Physical examination shows no abnormalities. The result of a urine pregnancy test is negative. The physician explains that hormone therapy likely will help and explains the risks to the patient. Which of the following is the next most appropriate physician statement?

options.text: "Could you tell me your thoughts about the hormone treatment option we have discussed?"
"I have many patients with similar symptoms, and everyone responds to hormone therapy differently."
"I will give you some written information to review, and then I can answer any remaining questions."
"If your symptoms are really severe, the risk of hormone therapy may be worth it.”
"Would you like me to tell you what I think you should do?"

explanation:
After explaining the benefits and risks of hormone therapy, the physician should practice shared decision-making by eliciting the patient's own perspective. Option A ("Could you tell me your thoughts about the hormone treatment option we have discussed?") invites her values and concerns into the decision and is the most appropriate next step.

Distractors: Option B normalizes the experience but does not elicit the patient's preferences or advance shared decision-making. Option C provides written information but defers the conversation without first assessing the patient's understanding or values. Option D steers the patient toward treatment by suggesting severe symptoms justify the risks, rather than exploring her individual risk tolerance. Option E offers the physician's opinion before understanding the patient's own thoughts and concerns, undermining patient autonomy and shared decision-making.
subject: General Principles
concept_fingerprint: shared decision making physician patient communication

text: A randomized controlled trial is conducted to assess the risk for development of gastrointestinal adverse effects using azithromycin compared with erythromycin in the treatment of pertussis in children. Of the 100 children with pertussis enrolled, 50 receive azithromycin, and 50 receive erythromycin. Results show vomiting among 5 patients in the azithromycin group, compared with 15 patients in the erythromycin group. Which of the following best represents the absolute risk reduction for vomiting among patients in the azithromycin group?
explanation: Absolute risk reduction equals the event rate in the control (erythromycin) group minus the event rate in the treatment (azithromycin) group. Vomiting occurred in 15/50 = 0.30 with erythromycin and 5/50 = 0.10 with azithromycin, so the ARR is 0.30 − 0.10 = 0.20. (C) 0.33 and (D) 0.67 correspond to relative measures, and (A) 0.1 and (E) 0.8 reflect a single group's rate or its complement rather than the difference.
subject: General Principles

text: A 34-year-old woman with a 10-year history of hepatitis C comes to the physician because of progressive fatigue during the past month. Her vital signs are within normal limits. Physical examination shows that the liver is not palpable. Serum studies show: Albumin 3 g/dL Total bilirubin 1.8 mg/dL Alkaline phosphatase 115 U/L AST 53 U/L ALT 48 U/L A liver biopsy specimen shows focal areas of hepatocellular injury with infiltration of lymphocytes and early fibrosis. Which of the following mechanisms is the most likely cause of the ongoing hepatocyte injury in this patient?

options.text: Foreign peptides bound to class I MHC molecules are recognized by CD4+ T lymphocytes
Foreign peptides bound to class I MHC molecules are recognized by CD8+ T lymphocytes
Foreign peptides bound to class II MHC molecules are recognized by CD8+ T lymphocytes
Self-peptides bound to class I MHC molecules are recognized by CD8+ T lymphocytes
Self-peptides bound to class II MHC molecules are recognized by CD4+ T lymphocytes

explanation:
In chronic hepatitis C, ongoing hepatocyte injury is primarily immune-mediated rather than directly cytopathic. Virally infected hepatocytes process and present foreign (viral) peptides on **class I MHC molecules**. These peptide-MHC I complexes are recognized by **CD8+ cytotoxic T lymphocytes**, which then kill the infected hepatocytes.

**Distractors:**
- **(A)** incorrectly pairs class I MHC with CD4+ T lymphocytes; CD4+ cells recognize antigens presented on MHC class II.
- **(C)** incorrectly pairs class II MHC with CD8+ T lymphocytes; class II molecules present antigens to CD4+ helper T cells.
- **(D)** describes recognition of **self-peptides** on class I MHC by CD8+ T cells, which characterizes autoimmune mechanisms (e.g., autoimmune hepatitis), not viral injury.
- **(E)** describes recognition of **self-peptides** on class II MHC by CD4+ T cells, which also characterizes autoimmune processes rather than immune-mediated viral clearance.
subject: GI
concept_fingerprint: MHC I CD8 viral hepatitis cytotoxicity

text: A 50-year-old woman comes to the physician for a follow-up examination. Her blood pressure was 145/100 mm Hg and 145/95 mm Hg, respectively, at two previous visits. Today, her pulse is 75/min, respirations are 15/min, and blood pressure is 150/95 mm Hg. Physical examination shows no other abnormalities. If left untreated, which of the following is most likely to decrease in this patient?
explanation: In sustained, untreated hypertension, the arterial baroreceptors reset to the higher pressure and their afferent firing (baroreceptor output) decreases over time, blunting reflex buffering of blood pressure. The heart, in contrast, adapts by increasing left ventricular wall thickness (concentric hypertrophy); consequently, left ventricular wall thickness (D) increases. This hypertrophy also raises left ventricular stiffness during diastole (B), left ventricular stroke work (C), and myocardial oxygen consumption (E). Therefore, baroreceptor output (A) is the only parameter listed that decreases.
subject: Cardiovascular

text: A 62-year-old man comes to the physician for a follow-up examination after he was diagnosed with chronic inflammatory interstitial pneumonitis. Following pulmonary function testing, a biopsy specimen of the affected area of the lungs is obtained. Compared with a healthy man, analysis of this patient's biopsy specimen is most likely to show which of the following patterns of changes in the cell populations of alveoli?
explanation:
In chronic interstitial pneumonitis with fibrosis, the delicate type I pneumocytes that line most of the alveolar surface are injured and decrease in number, while type II pneumocytes proliferate (increase) as the reparative/stem-like cell population, and fibroblasts increase as they deposit collagen and drive fibrosis. This ↓ type I, ↑ type II, ↑ fibroblast pattern corresponds to option E.

**Distractors:** Options A–D show increased type I pneumocytes, which is inconsistent with destructive injury to the alveolar lining. Options C, D, G, and H show decreased type II pneumocytes, but these cells characteristically proliferate to repopulate injured epithelium. Options B, F, and H show decreased fibroblasts, which cannot account for the collagen deposition and fibrosis characteristic of this disease.
subject: Respiratory

text: A 31-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes mellitus comes to the physician because of an oozing, foul-smelling wound on her foot for 2 days. Physical examination shows a 4-cm, necrotizing wound with a purplish black discoloration over the heel. Crepitant bullae producing profuse amounts of serous drainage are seen. A Gram stain of a tissue biopsy specimen shows gram-positive rods. The causal organism most likely produces which of the following virulence factors?
explanation:
A diabetic patient with a rapidly necrotizing wound showing crepitus (gas), purplish-black discoloration, and gram-positive rods has clostridial myonecrosis (gas gangrene), most often due to *Clostridium perfringens*. Its principal virulence factor is α-toxin, a lecithinase (phospholipase C) that degrades cell membranes, causing tissue necrosis and hemolysis.

**Distractors:**
- **(A) Endotoxin:** Lipopolysaccharide is a component of the outer membrane of gram-negative bacteria, not produced by gram-positive rods such as *C. perfringens*.
- **(B) Fimbriae:** These adhesive appendages are associated with many gram-negative bacteria (e.g., *E. coli*) and some gram-positive organisms, but they are not the principal toxin responsible for the rapidly necrotizing lesions of gas gangrene.
- **(C) Pneumolysin:** This pore-forming toxin is produced by *Streptococcus pneumoniae* and contributes to pneumonia and meningitis pathogenesis; it is not associated with clostridial myonecrosis.
- **(D) Polysaccharide capsule:** A major virulence factor for encapsulated pathogens (e.g., *Streptococcus pneumoniae*, *Haemophilus influenzae*, *Neisseria meningitidis*) that evades phagocytosis, but it is not the key factor in *C. perfringens* tissue destruction.
subject: MSK/Skin
concept_fingerprint: C perfringens alpha toxin gas gangrene

text: A 4-month-old boy with severe combined immunodeficiency receives a bone marrow transplant. Six days later, he develops a widespread, erythematous, maculopapular rash over the trunk. Examination of a skin biopsy specimen shows diffuse vacuolar degeneration of basal epidermal cells with a mononuclear inflammatory cell infiltrate. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient’s rash?
explanation:
This infant with severe combined immunodeficiency developed a maculopapular rash days after a bone marrow transplant, and the biopsy shows vacuolar degeneration of basal keratinocytes with a mononuclear infiltrate—classic acute graft-versus-host disease (GVHD). Immunocompetent donor T lymphocytes recognize the immunocompromised recipient's tissues as foreign and attack the skin, gut, and liver.

Distractors: Fixed drug eruption (A) typically causes well-demarcated, hyperpigmented patches rather than diffuse vacuolar basal-layer injury. Immune complex deposition (C) produces vasculitis or nephritis, not basal keratinocyte vacuolar degeneration. Mast cell degranulation (D) causes urticaria via histamine release without mononuclear infiltrate or basal-cell vacuolar change. Staphylococcal folliculitis (E) is a neutrophilic bacterial infection of hair follicles, not a diffuse mononuclear infiltrate with basal vacuolar degeneration.
subject: Hemat/Lymph/Immune

text: A 37-year-old woman with right lower extremity edema is evaluated because of the sudden onset of shortness of breath and pleuritic chest pain. A diagnosis of pulmonary embolism is made. Which of the following signs, if present on physical examination, would be the most specific indicator of pulmonary arterial hypertension in this patient?
explanation: A loud pulmonic component of the second heart sound (P2 louder than A2) is the most specific physical finding of pulmonary arterial hypertension, because elevated pulmonary artery pressure forces the pulmonic valve closed more forcefully. (A) Increased jugular venous pressure, (C) peripheral edema, and (D) an S3 reflect right heart strain or failure but are nonspecific. (E) Pulmonary crackles suggest parenchymal or alveolar disease rather than elevated pulmonary arterial pressure.
subject: Cardiovascular

text: A 43-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes mellitus is brought to the emergency department because of a 12-hour history of nausea and vomiting. She says that it began after drinking champagne at a birthday party the previous night. Three days ago, she was diagnosed with Trichomonas vaginalis infection, and a 5-day course of metronidazole was initiated. Current medications also include acetaminophen, lisinopril, hydrochlorothiazide, and metformin. Her temperature is 37.2°C (99°F), pulse is 110/min, and blood pressure is 125/82 mm Hg. Physical examination shows pallor and dry mucous membranes. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's nausea and vomiting?
explanation:
This patient developed nausea and vomiting after drinking alcohol while taking metronidazole. Metronidazole inhibits aldehyde dehydrogenase, producing a disulfiram-like reaction in which acetaldehyde accumulates and causes flushing, nausea, vomiting, and tachycardia.

**Distractors:**
- **(B) Gastritis secondary to alcohol:** Alcoholic gastritis would not be triggered so specifically in this setting.
- **(C) Lactic acidosis secondary to metformin:** Metformin-associated lactic acidosis is rare and not precipitated by this exposure.
- **(D) Metronidazole-induced hepatotoxicity:** Would present with hepatic dysfunction rather than this acute post-alcohol reaction.
- **(E) Viral hepatitis:** Would present with hepatic dysfunction rather than this acute post-alcohol reaction.
subject: General Principles

text: A 45-year-old man comes to the physician because of right shoulder pain that began after he chopped wood 2 days ago. Examination of the right upper extremity shows no obvious bone deformities or point tenderness. The pain is reproduced when the patient is asked to externally rotate the shoulder against resistance; there is no weakness. In addition to the teres minor, inflammation of which of the following tendons is most likely in this patient?
explanation: Pain reproduced by resisted external rotation of the shoulder implicates the external rotators of the rotator cuff. Along with the teres minor, the infraspinatus is the primary external rotator and is the tendon most likely inflamed here. **(D) Supraspinatus** initiates abduction. **(C) Subscapularis** is an internal rotator. **(B) Pectoralis** and **(E) Trapezius** are not rotator cuff muscles responsible for resisted external rotation.
subject: MSK/Skin

text: A 44-year-old man comes to the physician because of a 6-week history of progressive numbness of his feet. Two months ago, he completed a course of chemotherapy, including vincristine, for small cell lung carcinoma. Physical examination shows muscle weakness of the distal portion of the feet and absent ankle jerk reflexes. Sensation is decreased over the distal portions of the lower extremities. This patient's findings are most likely caused by which of the following mechanisms?

options.text: Apoptosis of dorsal root ganglion neurons
Decreased expression of myelin protein in Schwann cells

explanation: Vincristine causes a dose-dependent peripheral neuropathy by binding tubulin and depolymerizing microtubules, which disrupts axonal transport in long peripheral nerves and produces the distal sensory loss, weakness, and lost ankle reflexes seen here. (A) Apoptosis of dorsal root ganglion neurons, (B) respiratory chain blockade, (C) decreased Schwann cell myelin protein, and (E) inhibition of synaptic vesicle endocytosis describe mechanisms of other toxins or diseases, not the antimicrotubule action of vincristine.
subject: Behavioral/Nervous & Special Senses

text: A 10-year-old girl is brought to the office by her mother because her school nurse thinks that she may have Marfan syndrome. She is at the 95th percentile for height and 25th percentile for weight. Physical examination shows a narrow palate with dental crowding, long slender extremities, and joint laxity. Molecular testing for FBN1 shows a single nucleotide difference that does not change the amino acid at that locus. Her mother is 163 cm (5 ft 4 in) tall. There is no clinical evidence of Marfan syndrome in the mother, but she has the same single nucleotide change as the patient. The same nucleotide change is found in 15 of 200 individuals without Marfan syndrome. Which of the following best describes the single nucleotide change in the patient and her mother?

options.text: It is a disease-causing mutation in the patient and her mother
It is a sequence variant of unknown significance
It will change the folding of the protein
It will result in a truncated protein

explanation: This is a synonymous (silent) single-nucleotide change that does not alter the amino acid, is present in an unaffected parent, and is found in 15 of 200 (7.5%) people without Marfan syndrome. A variant occurring at greater than 1% frequency in the population and not tracking with disease is a polymorphism, not a pathogenic mutation. Because it does not change the amino acid and is common in unaffected individuals, it is not (A) disease-causing, (C) a variant of unknown significance, or one that (D) alters folding or (E) truncates the protein.
subject: General Principles

text: A 26-year-old woman comes to a busy emergency department because of a 2-day history of runny nose. She has no history of major medical illness and takes no medications. Her vital signs are within normal limits. The patient has to wait 6 hours before she is seen by a physician. She is angry with the staff and says the only reason she had to wait this long is because she does not have insurance. In addition to apologizing to the patient, which of the following is the most appropriate opening remark by the physician?

options.text: "It is harsh to suggest that you waited because you don’t have insurance, but how can we help you feel better today?"
"It sounds like you are angry; shall I come back in a few minutes?"
"Our wait time has nothing to do with insurance, so let’s talk about the reason you are here."
"The reason you waited so long is because we need to triage by severity."
"Thank you for waiting. How can I help you today?"

explanation:
After apologizing, the most appropriate opening remark is professional, nondefensive, and refocuses on the patient's medical concern. Option E ("Thank you for waiting. How can I help you today?") briefly acknowledges the long wait without being defensive, implicitly validates the patient's frustration, and immediately redirects the encounter toward her clinical issue, thereby preserving the therapeutic relationship.

**Distractors:**
- **A** is incorrect because telling the patient her suggestion is "harsh" is confrontational and defensive; it challenges her perception rather than moving forward with care.
- **B** is incorrect because offering to return later postpones evaluation and may be perceived as dismissive or punitive.
- **C** is incorrect because directly contradicting the patient's belief ("nothing to do with insurance") is defensive and risks escalating conflict.
- **D** is incorrect because explaining triage policy deflects responsibility and does not acknowledge the patient's emotional experience; it is perceived as defensive justification rather than empathetic engagement.
subject: Behavioral/Nervous & Special Senses

text: A 26-year-old man is brought to the emergency department by ambulance 30 minutes after being shot in the leg. He is unconscious and appears markedly pale. His pulse is 120/min, respirations are 16/min, and blood pressure is 80/60 mm Hg. Compared with a healthy adult, which of the following findings is most likely in this patient?
explanation:
This patient is in hemorrhagic (hypovolemic) shock. The low arterial pressure reduces arterial baroreceptor firing (↓), which triggers reflex sympathetic activation that increases systemic vascular resistance (↑) and pulmonary vascular resistance (↑). The fall in capillary hydrostatic pressure shifts the Starling balance toward net absorption of interstitial fluid into the capillaries (autotransfusion). This ↓ baroreceptor firing, ↑ systemic resistance, ↑ pulmonary resistance, absorption pattern corresponds to option D.

Distractors: Options suggesting increased baroreceptor firing (A, B, C) are incorrect because low arterial pressure decreases baroreceptor firing. Options suggesting decreased systemic or pulmonary vascular resistance (B, C, F) are incorrect because sympathetic activation increases both resistances. Options suggesting filtration (A, C, E) are incorrect because reduced capillary hydrostatic pressure promotes net absorption, not filtration.
subject: Cardiovascular

text: A 36-year-old man with profound intellectual disability is brought to the physician by staff at his facility because of increasing abdominal girth during the past 2 weeks. He is unable to speak, and no medical history is currently available. Physical examination shows a protuberant abdomen with a fluid wave and shifting dullness. There are no signs of trauma to the area. Laboratory studies show no abnormalities. A CT scan of the abdomen is shown. Fluid is present in which of the following areas as indicated by the arrow?
explanation:
The arrow indicates ascitic fluid collecting in the omental bursa (lesser sac), the peritoneal space located posterior to the stomach and anterior to the pancreas. Free peritoneal fluid in a supine patient commonly tracks into this potential space.

**Distractors:**
- **(A) Epiploic foramen:** This is the opening (foramen of Winslow) that connects the greater and lesser sacs; it is not a recess where fluid accumulates.
