text: A 45-year-old man is brought to the clinic by his wife because of a 6-month history of progressive weakness; he also has had dysphagia and a 4.5-kg (10-lb) weight loss during this period. He has had to use a wheelchair during the past 3 weeks because of the weakness. He has no other history of major medical illness and takes no medications. He is a former financial analyst and has no known toxin exposures. He does not smoke or drink alcoholic beverages. He is 183 cm (6 ft) tall and now weighs 68 kg (150 lb); BMI is 20 kg/m2. His temperature is 37.0°C (98.6°F), pulse is 88/min, respirations are 18/min, and blood pressure is 138/78 mm Hg. He is mentally alert. Physical examination shows muscle fasciculations of the upper extremities and weakness of the lower extremities. The remainder of the physical examination is most likely to show which of the following additional findings in this patient?
explanation:
This patient presents with progressive weakness, dysphagia, weight loss, upper extremity fasciculations (lower motor neuron signs), and lower extremity weakness (upper motor neuron signs) in the absence of sensory, visual, or cognitive deficits. This pattern is classic for amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS). Because ALS involves degeneration of both upper and lower motor neurons, denervation from lower motor neuron loss produces muscle atrophy. Therefore, additional examination is most likely to show atrophy.

**Distractors:**
- **(B) Decreased visual acuity:** ALS does not involve the visual pathways or cranial nerves responsible for vision.
- **(C) Loss of proprioception:** ALS is a motor neuron disease that characteristically spares sensory pathways, including proprioception.
- **(D) Presence of palmomental reflex:** A frontal release reflex suggests frontal lobe or diffuse cortical pathology, not ALS.
- **(E) Ptosis:** Ptosis typically indicates neuromuscular junction disorders (e.g., myasthenia gravis) or oculomotor nerve pathology, not ALS.
subject: Behavioral/Nervous & Special Senses

text: A new severe respiratory illness caused by a newly identified virus is discovered. Which of the following properties of a killed vaccine relative to a live vaccine is the most appropriate rationale for developing a killed vaccine for this illness?

options.text: Avoids the concern for reversion to virulence
Is less likely to require subsequent boosters for lifelong immunity
Is most likely to generate mucosal immunity
Requires little safety monitoring to ensure inactivation

explanation: The principal advantage of a killed (inactivated) vaccine over a live attenuated vaccine is that it cannot revert to a virulent form, making it safer—an important consideration for a newly identified, severe pathogen. Live vaccines, by contrast, (B) tend to produce faster and (C) more durable immunity and (D) better mucosal immunity. (E) Inactivated vaccines actually require careful safety monitoring to confirm complete inactivation, so that is not their advantage.
subject: Hemat/Lymph/Immune

text: A 33-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a 2-day history of mild nausea, increased urinary urgency and frequency, and constipation. She also has had a 4.5-kg (10-lb) weight loss during the past 2 weeks and a 3-week history of vaginal bleeding. Pelvic examination shows a nodular cervix with an irregular, friable posterior lip, and a rock-hard, irregular, immobile pelvic mass that extends across the pelvis. Examination of biopsy specimens from the cervix and anterior wall of the vagina show well-differentiated keratinizing squamous cell carcinoma. Which of the following best describes the pathogenesis of this patient's disease?

options.text: Insertion of viral promotors adjacent to cellular growth factor genes
Transactivation of cellular growth factor genes by TAX
Translocation of CMYC to an Ig gene promoter

explanation: Cervical squamous cell carcinoma is driven by high-risk human papillomavirus (HPV). The viral E6 protein promotes degradation and inactivation of cellular p53 (and E7 inactivates Rb), removing tumor-suppressor control. (B) Insertional activation of growth factor genes describes other retroviral oncogenesis. (C) Specialized transduction is a bacteriophage mechanism. (D) TAX transactivation occurs in HTLV-1. (E) The CMYC–immunoglobulin translocation characterizes Burkitt lymphoma—none is the mechanism of HPV-driven cervical cancer.
subject: Reproductive/Endocrine

text: A 54-year-old woman with a 40-year history of type 1 diabetes mellitus comes to the office for a follow-up examination. She is receiving hemodialysis for end-stage renal disease while awaiting a kidney transplant. As part of her regimen, she also receives regular injections of a drug that induces reticulocyte release from the bone marrow and stimulates a cytokine receptor that signals via the JAK/STAT pathway. This patient is most likely receiving which of the following drugs?
explanation: A drug that triggers reticulocyte release from the marrow and signals through a cytokine receptor using the JAK/STAT pathway is erythropoietin, which is used to treat the anemia of chronic kidney disease in dialysis patients. (B) Filgrastim (G-CSF) and (E) sargramostim (GM-CSF) stimulate granulocyte lineages, (C) IL-2 expands lymphocytes, and (D) platelet-derived growth factor acts via receptor tyrosine kinases rather than driving erythropoiesis.
subject: Hemat/Lymph/Immune

text: During a clinical study examining the effects of exercise, men between the ages of 20 and 30 years are evaluated during a 15-minute session on a treadmill. The average pulse for the last 2 minutes of the session is 175/min. During the last minute of exercise, various measurements are taken. Compared with the measurement before the session, which of the following is most likely to be decreased?
explanation: During vigorous exercise, vasodilation of skeletal muscle arterioles markedly lowers total peripheral resistance, which is therefore the parameter most likely to be decreased. In contrast, cardiac output, oxygen consumption, pulse pressure, stroke volume, and systolic blood pressure all increase during dynamic exercise to meet metabolic demand.
subject: Cardiovascular

text: An 8-year-old boy is brought to the office by his mother because of a 3-day history of fever, sore throat, and itchy eyes. He just returned from a weeklong summer camp that included hiking trips and swimming lessons in the camp- owned swimming pool. He has no history of major medical illness and receives no medications. He appears tired. His temperature is 39.4°C (102.9°F); other vital signs are within normal limits. Physical examination shows conjunctival injection and discharge and oropharyngeal erythema. The public health department reports an outbreak of similar symptoms among the other campers and camp volunteers. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient’s symptoms?
explanation: Fever, pharyngitis, and conjunctivitis occurring as a swimming pool–associated outbreak is the classic presentation of pharyngoconjunctival fever caused by adenovirus, which spreads readily in pools and summer camps. **(A) Adenovirus** is the most likely cause. **(B) Cytomegalovirus** and **(C) Epstein-Barr virus** typically cause mononucleosis-type illness. **(D) Influenza virus** causes respiratory illness without this distinctive conjunctivitis-pharyngitis pool outbreak pattern. **(E) West Nile virus** is mosquito-borne and causes neuroinvasive disease rather than pharyngoconjunctival symptoms.
subject: Multisystem

text: A 44-year-old woman comes to the office because of a 10-month history of wide red streaks over her lower trunk and significant weight gain in her face and abdomen. Although her appetite has increased, she has noticed that her arms and legs have become thinner. Which of the following additional findings are most likely in this patient?

options.text: Hypoglycemia and fat pads between the scapulae
Jaundice and thinning of the skin

explanation:
Wide purple/red abdominal striae, central (facial and truncal) weight gain, and thin (wasting) extremities indicate Cushing syndrome from cortisol excess. Expected additional findings include hypertension (from cortisol's mineralocorticoid-like and vascular effects) and proximal muscle weakness.

**Distractors:** (A) is incorrect because cortisol excess causes hypokalemia, not hyperkalemia. (C) Hypocalcemia, (D) hypoglycemia, and (E) jaundice are not features of cortisol excess; cortisol excess causes hyperglycemia.
subject: Reproductive/Endocrine

text: A 12-year-old boy is brought to the physician by his mother because of a 1-month history of pain below the left knee. His mother says, "He can usually walk around, but he hasn't been able to play in any of his soccer games since this all began." Examination of the left knee shows warmth, swelling, and tenderness. An x-ray of the knee is shown. Which of the following structures is attached to the abnormal anterior tibial area?
explanation: This adolescent athlete with pain, warmth, and swelling over the tibial tubercle has Osgood-Schlatter disease (traction apophysitis of the tibial tuberosity). The patellar ligament inserts on the tibial tubercle, and repetitive quadriceps traction through this ligament causes the abnormal anterior tibial changes. (A) The anterior and (E) posterior cruciate ligaments attach within the joint, and (B) the gastrocnemius, (D) popliteus, and (F) soleus do not attach to the tibial tubercle.
subject: MSK/Skin

text: A 65-year-old retired man comes to the office for a health maintenance examination. He has no history of major medical illness and takes no medications. He lives in a single-family home with his cat and dog. He spends much of his time in his basement woodworking shop. He does not smoke. His temperature is 37.0°C (98.6°F), pulse is 84/min, respirations are 12/min, and blood pressure is 138/88 mm Hg. Physical examination shows no cyanosis. The lungs are clear. Cardiac examination shows no abnormalities. Extremity examination shows no edema. The patient wishes to mitigate his risk for pulmonary disease. This patient is at increased risk for lung cancer because of which of the following environmental exposures?
explanation: This patient spends prolonged time in a basement, the area of a home where radon gas accumulates. Radon-222 is a radioactive decay product of uranium in soil; it is the leading environmental cause of lung cancer and the second leading cause overall after tobacco smoking. Indoor cleaning chemicals, pet dander, polyurethane, and sawdust are not established causes of lung cancer comparable to radon exposure.
subject: Respiratory

text: A 54-year-old man comes to the physician for a follow-up examination 10 days after undergoing a stereotactic brain operation to remove a small tumor. The operation was successful. During the procedure, he was under conscious sedation. The patient recalls that at one point during the operation he experienced a sudden, intense feeling of overwhelming fear. Which of the following areas of the brain was most likely stimulated at that time?
explanation: A sudden, intense feeling of overwhelming fear evoked by intraoperative stimulation localizes to the amygdala, the limbic structure central to processing fear and threat. (B) The hippocampus mediates memory formation, (C) the mammillary body is involved in memory circuits, (D) the prefrontal cortex governs executive function, and (E) the thalamus relays sensory information—none produces the discrete fear response attributed to the amygdala.
subject: Behavioral/Nervous & Special Senses

text: A 30-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a 2-day history of abdominal pain. She has a history of recurrent upper respiratory tract infections, sinusitis, and pancreatitis. She has thick nasal secretions. She says that her sweat is salty and crystallizes on her skin. Her vital signs are within normal limits. Physical examination shows epigastric tenderness. Genetic testing for the 36 most common mutations shows a detectable mutation (G551D) in one allele of the CFTR gene. Which of the following best explains this patient's clinical phenotype?

options.text: Loss of heterozygosity of the CFTR gene has occurred in the pancreas
Only one G551D allele is needed in CFTR
The patient is a CFTR obligate carrier
The patient's CFTR mutation is unrelated to her clinical phenotype
The second CFTR mutation was not detected by the testing obtained

explanation: This patient has a clear cystic fibrosis phenotype (salty, crystallizing sweat, recurrent sinopulmonary infections, pancreatitis), yet a targeted panel for the 36 most common mutations detected only one CFTR mutation (G551D). Because CF is autosomal recessive and her phenotype indicates two affected alleles, the most likely explanation is that the second CFTR mutation is present but was not among the mutations tested by the limited panel. (A) Loss of heterozygosity, (B) a single allele being sufficient, (C) carrier status, and (D) an unrelated mutation do not fit a symptomatic recessive disease.
subject: Multisystem
concept_fingerprint: CFTR second mutation missed by panel

text: A 74-year-old man with mild chronic obstructive pulmonary disease comes to the physician for a follow-up examination. Current medications include a short-acting β2-adrenergic agonist by metered-dose inhaler as needed. Physical examination shows no abnormalities. At the end of the examination, he tells the physician, "I enjoy coming to see you because you remind me of my daughter. She died 35 years ago this month." He has been a patient of this physician for 5 years. Which of the following is the most appropriate response by the physician?

options.text: "I may have to refer you to another physician who doesn't remind you of your daughter so you can focus more on your medical condition and its treatment."
"I'd like to refer you to a grief counselor so that you can work out your unresolved feelings about your daughter's death."
"I'm sorry you lost your daughter. Unfortunately, since we only have a limited amount of time, we must now move on to your medical condition."
"That makes me feel a little uncomfortable. I hope you understand."
"You must miss your daughter very much. Tell me about her."

explanation: This patient is sharing a personal grief, and the most therapeutic response is empathic and invites him to elaborate: "You must miss your daughter very much. Tell me about her." This acknowledges his emotion and strengthens the therapeutic relationship. (A) Referring him away, (C) cutting him off to move on, and (D) expressing the physician's discomfort are dismissive. (B) An immediate grief-counseling referral is premature for a long-grieving patient who is simply expressing a feeling in the context of an established relationship.
subject: Behavioral/Nervous & Special Senses

text: A 9-month-old boy is brought to the office by his mother for a well-child examination. He was born at 32 weeks’ gestation because of spontaneous rupture of membranes. Growth and development are appropriate for age. His mother says he can sit without support and is interactive. She is concerned that he still takes two to three 1-hour naps daily. He goes to sleep at 7 PM and awakens at 7 AM. She says he also awakens and cries at least once nightly and settles back to sleep after drinking a bottle of formula. Physical examination shows no abnormalities. Which of the following is the most likely explanation for this patient’s sleep pattern?
explanation:
At 9 months of age, taking two to three daytime naps and having one brief nighttime awakening is a normal sleep pattern. The infant is easily soothed back to sleep with a bottle, indicating a learned sleep association rather than organic disease. His growth, development, and physical examination are all normal, making normal development the best explanation.

Distractors: Gastroesophageal reflux would likely present with vomiting, irritability, or arching after feeds. Hypoglycemia would cause sweating, jitteriness, or seizures rather than a single nightly awakening that resolves with feeding. Obstructive sleep apnea typically presents with snoring, gasping, or daytime somnolence. Parasomnias such as night terrors occur later in childhood and involve partial arousal with inconsolable crying rather than easy soothing with a bottle.
subject: Behavioral/Nervous & Special Senses

text: A 32-year-old man comes to the office because of a 2-year history of abnormal movements of his hands that are worse when he feels angry or depressed. His maternal grandmother and mother, both now deceased, had similar symptoms with onset at the ages of 53 years and 42 years, respectively. Neurologic examination shows normal muscle strength, bulk, and tone. There is no intention tremor or dysmetria. Sensation is intact. He is unable to fix his gaze on one point or protrude his tongue for more than 30 seconds. Deep tendon reflexes are hyperactive. Mental status examination shows no abnormalities. This patient most likely has an anatomic abnormality in which of the following locations?
explanation: This patient has an autosomal dominant disorder with anticipation (progressively earlier onset across generations: 53, then 42, then his 30s), chorea worsened by emotion, motor impersistence (inability to sustain tongue protrusion or fixed gaze), and hyperreflexia—Huntington disease. The underlying degeneration occurs in the basal ganglia, particularly atrophy of the caudate nucleus. Distractors: (B) Cerebellar lesions cause intention tremor, dysmetria, and ataxia, which are absent here. (C) Dorsal spinal column lesions impair vibration and proprioception, which are intact in this patient. (D) Frontal lobe lesions can cause personality changes or executive dysfunction, but not chorea or motor impersistence as the primary feature. (E) Lateral spinal column (corticospinal tract) lesions cause weakness and spasticity, not choreiform movements.
subject: Behavioral/Nervous & Special Senses
